PSA.51.7: David asks God to make him clean again, using an image of being washed whiter than snow.
PSA.51.17: David says that what God truly wants is not animal sacrifices but a humble, broken heart.
PSA.52.8: Contrasting himself with a powerful man who trusted in his wealth, David pictures himself as an olive tree flourishing in God's house.
PSA.55.16: Betrayed by a close friend, David says he will call on God, confident that God will save him.
PSA.56.9: Hunted by enemies, David says that whenever he cries out, he knows God is on his side.
PSA.57.2: Hiding from King Saul in a cave, David cries out to God, who he says will fulfill his purpose for him.
PSA.57.10: Still in the cave, David praises God's love as reaching higher than the heavens.
PSA.59.16: While Saul's men watch his house to kill him, David says he will sing each morning about God's strength and love.
PSA.61.3: Praying from what feels like the ends of the earth, David remembers that God has always been his refuge and strong tower.
PSA.61.4: Far from home, David asks to live in God's presence forever, sheltered under his wings like a young bird.

JOB.30.20: After recalling his former honor, Job describes his present misery and tells God that his cries for help seem to go unanswered.
JOB.30.26: Contrasting his past blessings with his present suffering, Job says that when he looked for good and light, only evil and darkness came.
JOB.42.3: After God speaks to him from the whirlwind, Job repeats God's question back and admits he spoke about things far too wonderful for him.
PRO.3.27: Solomon, teaching his son, tells him not to hold back good from those who are owed it when he has the power to help.
PRO.11.24: In one of his proverbs, Solomon contrasts a person who gives freely and still prospers with one who holds back and ends up in need.
PRO.12.16: Solomon contrasts a fool who shows his anger immediately with a sensible person who lets an insult pass.
PRO.14.10: In a proverb about the inner life, Solomon observes that each heart knows its own bitterness and joy in ways no outsider can fully share.
PRO.14.13: Solomon observes in this proverb that laughter can hide an aching heart, and that joy can give way to sorrow.
PRO.15.4: In one of his proverbs about speech, Solomon contrasts gentle words that bring life with twisted words that crush a person's spirit.
PRO.15.16: Solomon compares a modest life lived in reverence for God with great wealth that comes bundled with trouble.
PRO.15.18: In this proverb about temper, Solomon contrasts a hot-headed person who starts fights with a patient one who calms them down.
PRO.18.14: Solomon observes in this proverb that a person's spirit can carry them through illness, but a crushed spirit is far harder to bear.
PRO.18.19: In a proverb about family conflict, Solomon says a brother who has been wronged is harder to win back than a walled city.
PRO.19.23: Solomon says in this proverb that reverence for the LORD leads to life, letting a person rest content and safe from harm.
PRO.20.3: In a proverb about quarrels, Solomon says it brings a person honor to step away from a dispute, while any fool rushes into one.
PRO.20.9: Solomon poses this question as a proverb, asking whether anyone can honestly claim to have a clean heart and be free of sin.
PRO.21.23: In one of his proverbs about speech, Solomon says that a person who guards what they say keeps themselves out of trouble.
PRO.22.2: Solomon observes in this proverb that rich and poor people stand on common ground, since the LORD made them all.
PRO.23.4: In a series of sayings for his son, Solomon warns against wearing oneself out chasing riches and urges the wisdom to hold back.
PRO.24.29: Solomon warns his son in this saying against vowing to pay someone back for what they have done to him.
PRO.29.23: In a proverb copied by King Hezekiah's scribes from Solomon's sayings, pride is said to bring a person low, while humility leads to honor.
PRO.30.2: Opening his sayings, a lesser-known figure named Agur humbly admits that he feels he lacks ordinary human understanding.
PRO.31.8: King Lemuel's mother, teaching her son how a king should rule, urges him to speak up for people who have no voice of their own.
ECC.1.9: Opening his reflections on life, the Preacher observes that the same things keep happening over and over, with nothing truly new.
ECC.1.18: After setting out to understand everything, the Preacher reports that gaining more wisdom and knowledge only brought him more grief.
ECC.2.11: After describing his great building projects, wealth, and pleasures, the Preacher looks back on it all and finds it empty.
ECC.2.22: Reflecting on having to leave his work to whoever comes after him, the Preacher asks what a person really gains from all their toil.
ECC.2.23: Still reflecting on the weariness of work, the Preacher describes a laborer whose days are full of grief and whose mind cannot rest at night.
ECC.4.1: The Preacher turns to look at oppression in the world and sees the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them.
ECC.5.10: Writing about wealth, the Preacher observes that people who love money never feel they have enough of it.
ECC.6.12: The Preacher asks who can know what is truly good for a person in a short, shadow-like life, or what will happen after they are gone.
ECC.7.3: In a string of sayings about mourning and death, the Preacher claims that sorrow can do more good for the heart than laughter.
ECC.7.10: The Preacher warns his readers against asking why the old days were better than the present, calling it an unwise question.
ECC.7.20: Reflecting on human goodness, the Preacher states plainly that no one on earth does only good and never sins.
ECC.7.21: The Preacher advises his readers not to take every word people say to heart, or they may overhear even a servant cursing them.
ECC.8.7: Reflecting on how little people can see ahead, the Preacher observes that no one knows what is coming or can tell anyone else.
ECC.9.7: Having reflected that the dead no longer share in life, the Preacher urges the living to eat and drink with a glad heart.
ECC.10.4: In a set of sayings about wisdom and rulers, the Preacher advises staying calm and keeping one's post when a ruler's anger flares.
ECC.11.7: Near the end of his reflections, the Preacher speaks of how sweet it is simply to be alive and see the light of the sun.
SNG.1.5: In this love poem, the young woman tells the daughters of Jerusalem that though her skin is darkened by the sun, she is still lovely.
SNG.1.15: In this love poem, the young man delights in his beloved, telling her how beautiful she is and comparing her eyes to doves.
SNG.2.11: The young woman recalls her beloved calling her to come away with him, because the winter and its rains are over and spring has come.
SNG.3.1: In this love poem, the young woman describes lying awake at night, searching for the man she loves and not finding him.
PSA.6.3: Weak and troubled to the bone, David cries out to God in this prayer, asking how long his distress must go on.
PSA.13.2: Feeling forgotten by God, David asks how long he must carry sorrow in his heart every day while his enemy gets the upper hand.
PSA.22.2: In a psalm that begins by asking why God has forsaken him, David says he cries out day and night without an answer or any rest.
PSA.22.10: Even while feeling abandoned in this psalm, David recalls that he has depended on God since the day he was born.
PSA.38.4: Sick in body and burdened by guilt, David tells God in this prayer that his sins feel like a weight too heavy to carry.
PSA.38.18: Near the end of a psalm about suffering caused by his own sin, David openly confesses his wrongdoing to God.
PSA.42.3: Far from the temple and longing for God, the sons of Korah describe crying day and night while others taunt, 'Where is your God?'
PSA.42.9: Longing for God while taunted by enemies, the sons of Korah pray to God as their rock, asking why he seems to have forgotten them.
PSA.44.24: After a crushing defeat of their nation, the sons of Korah ask God why he hides his face and seems to forget his people's suffering.
PSA.55.5: Betrayed by a close friend and surrounded by enemies in the city, David describes the fear and horror that have taken hold of him.
PSA.55.18: Though many oppose him and a close friend has betrayed him, David says God has rescued him unharmed from the battle against him.
PSA.69.1: Opening this psalm, David cries out to God for rescue, picturing himself sinking in floodwaters that have risen to his neck.
PSA.69.3: Hated without cause and sinking in trouble, David says he is worn out from crying and his eyes are failing as he waits for God.
PSA.69.5: In the middle of pleading for rescue from his enemies, David admits to God that his own foolishness and guilt are not hidden from God.
PSA.69.20: Mocked and shamed by enemies, David tells God that insults have broken his heart and he found no one to comfort him.
PSA.69.33: Near the end of this psalm, after pleading for rescue, David declares that the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his captive people.
PSA.77.2: Asaph describes a sleepless time of trouble when he reached out to the Lord all night and refused every comfort.
PSA.77.4: Asaph tells God in this psalm that he is too troubled to sleep and too distressed even to speak.
PSA.77.12: Troubled that God seems to have turned away from him, Asaph resolves to think back on all the mighty things God has done.
PSA.88.3: In one of the darkest psalms of the sons of Korah, the writer tells God his soul is full of troubles and his life is near the grave.
PSA.88.18: Ending this bleak psalm of the sons of Korah, the writer tells God that loved ones and friends are gone, leaving only darkness as company.
PSA.102.2: In a prayer the psalm's writer offers while overwhelmed, he begs God not to hide his face but to answer quickly in his day of distress.
PSA.102.7: Overwhelmed and alone, the psalm's writer tells God he lies awake at night like a lonely bird on a rooftop.
PSA.143.2: Pursued by an enemy, David asks God not to put him on trial, admitting that no living person is righteous before God.
PSA.143.4: With an enemy hunting him down, David tells God that his spirit is fainting and his heart is dismayed.
PSA.142.5: Written when David was hiding in a cave, this prayer has him cry out that the LORD alone is his refuge and portion in life.
PSA.10.12: Watching the wicked prey on the weak while God seems far off, the psalm's writer calls on God to rise and not forget the helpless.
PSA.32.3: David recalls in this psalm how, while he kept his sin hidden and unconfessed, he groaned all day and felt his body waste away.
PSA.51.3: In the psalm he wrote after the prophet Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba, David admits his sin is always in front of him.
PSA.51.9: In this psalm of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba, David asks God to look away from his sins and wipe out his guilt.
PSA.51.11: Repenting after his sin with Bathsheba, David begs God not to cast him away or take the Holy Spirit from him.
PSA.51.15: Still pleading for forgiveness in this psalm, David asks God to open his lips so he can declare his praise again.
PSA.41.4: Sick and surrounded by enemies hoping he will die, David recalls asking God for mercy and healing, admitting he had sinned.
PSA.78.38: Retelling Israel's history of rebellion in the wilderness, Asaph recalls how God still showed compassion and held back his anger.
PSA.79.8: After foreign nations have ruined Jerusalem and defiled the temple, Asaph asks God not to hold the people's past sins against them.
PSA.85.2: Praying for their people's restoration, the sons of Korah recall how God had once forgiven the nation and covered all its sin.
PSA.19.13: After praising God's law in this psalm, David asks God to keep him from deliberate sins so they will not rule over him.
PSA.90.8: In a prayer contrasting God's eternity with short human lives, Moses tells God that even his people's secret sins are laid bare before him.
PSA.109.4: Attacked with lies by people he had treated with love, David tells God that in return for his kindness they accuse him, yet he keeps praying.
PSA.34.3: After escaping from a Philistine king by pretending to be insane, David invites others to join him in praising the LORD together.
PSA.34.6: In this psalm written after his escape from a Philistine king, David calls himself a poor man whom the LORD heard and saved.
PSA.34.14: Teaching others what it means to fear the LORD, David urges them to turn from evil, do good, and actively pursue peace.
PSA.116.6: The psalm's writer, rescued from a brush with death, recalls how he was brought low and helpless until the LORD saved him.
PSA.116.17: Grateful to have been rescued from death, the psalm's writer promises to offer God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.
PSA.118.21: Entering the gates of the LORD after being rescued, the psalm's writer thanks God for answering him and saving him.
PSA.138.1: Opening this psalm, David declares that he will thank God with his whole heart and sing his praise even before the gods.
PSA.138.6: Praising God in this psalm, David observes that although the LORD is exalted, he takes notice of the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance.
PSA.100.2: In a short psalm calling the whole earth to worship, the psalm's writer invites everyone to serve the LORD gladly and come before him singing.
PSA.95.6: The psalm's writer calls the gathered worshippers to bow down and kneel together before the God who made them.
PSA.147.1: This psalm opens with a call to praise, as the writer declares how good and fitting it is to sing to God.
PSA.31.22: Looking back on a moment of panic, David admits he thought God had lost sight of him, yet God heard his cry for help.
PSA.120.1: In a pilgrim song sung on the way up to Jerusalem, the psalm's writer recalls calling to God in distress and being answered.
PSA.120.7: Living among hostile, deceitful neighbors, the psalm's writer says he wants peace, but they answer his every word with a push for war.
PSA.89.9: In a long psalm celebrating God's power and his promises to David, Ethan praises God as the one who calms the raging sea.
PSA.131.1: In a short pilgrim song, David tells God he has set aside pride and stopped chasing things too great for him.
PSA.3.6: Fleeing from his son Absalom with enemies all around, David says he will not fear even tens of thousands of them.
PSA.62.2: Waiting quietly on God while enemies try to topple him, David calls God his only rock, rescue and fortress.
PSA.121.4: In a pilgrim song for travelers heading to Jerusalem, the psalm's writer says the one who guards Israel never sleeps.
PSA.18.1: David opens this song, sung on the day God rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul, by declaring his love for God.
PSA.84.7: Picturing pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem, the sons of Korah describe them growing stronger until each stands before God in Zion.
PSA.1.2: Opening the whole book of Psalms, the writer describes the blessed person, who delights in God's law and thinks on it day and night.
PSA.16.7: Content with God as his portion, David praises the Lord who guides him, noting that even at night his inner thoughts teach him.
PSA.27.11: Surrounded by people who want to bring him down, David asks God to teach him his way and lead him on a smooth, safe path.
PSA.119.133: In the Bible's longest psalm, a meditation on God's word, the writer asks God to direct his steps and keep sin from ruling him.
PSA.119.67: Reflecting on a season of suffering in this long psalm about God's word, the writer admits he wandered before it and obeys now.
PSA.40.11: After recalling how God pulled him out of a pit, David, facing fresh troubles, asks God not to hold back his mercy.
PSA.119.97: In this long psalm devoted to God's word, the writer exclaims how much he loves God's law and thinks about it all day.
PSA.139.15: Marveling that God knows him completely, David says his body was never hidden from God, even while he was formed unseen in the womb.
PSA.118.22: In a psalm of thanks sung by one God rescued from enemies, the writer declares that the stone the builders threw out became the cornerstone.
PSA.73.3: Asaph confesses that he nearly lost his footing in faith because he envied proud people who seemed to prosper so easily.
PSA.89.49: After praising God's covenant with David, Ethan sees the royal line humbled and asks where God's promised faithful love has gone.
PSA.137.1: Remembering the exile, the psalm's writer describes the captives of Jerusalem sitting by Babylon's rivers and weeping for home.
PSA.137.4: When their Babylonian captors demand a song of Zion, the psalm's writer, speaking for the exiles, asks how they could sing God's songs in a foreign land.
PSA.94.17: Asking who will stand up for him against evildoers, the psalm's writer admits he would soon have died if God had not helped him.
PSA.57.7: Hiding from Saul in a cave, David declares that his heart is steady and resolves to sing and make music to God.
PSA.119.94: In this long psalm about God's word, the writer, with enemies waiting to destroy him, tells God he belongs to him and asks to be saved.
PSA.139.4: Reflecting on how thoroughly God knows him, David says God knows every word before it even reaches his tongue.
PSA.85.5: Having seen God restore the land before, the sons of Korah, facing new trouble, ask God whether his anger at his people will last forever.
PSA.107.22: After describing people God rescued from sickness brought on by their own folly, the psalm's writer calls them to offer thanks and tell his works.
PSA.119.35: In this long psalm about God's word, the writer asks God to guide him along the path of his commandments, where he finds joy.
PSA.35.18: Pleading for rescue from people repaying his kindness with malice, David promises to thank God publicly in the great assembly.
PSA.145.10: In a psalm of praise to God as King, David says all God has made will thank him and his faithful people will bless him.
ISA.12.1: Looking ahead to the day God gathers his scattered people, Isaiah gives them a song of praise because God's anger has turned to comfort.
ISA.30.19: After rebuking Judah for trusting Egypt instead of God, Isaiah promises the people of Jerusalem that their weeping will end when God answers.
ISA.38.14: Writing after he recovered from a deadly illness, King Hezekiah recalls how he moaned like a bird while begging God for help.
ISA.38.19: Having recovered from a deadly illness, King Hezekiah thanks God and says fathers will tell their children of his faithfulness.
ISA.40.2: Opening a new message of comfort, God commands that Jerusalem be spoken to tenderly and told that her hard service is over and her sin is paid for.
ISA.43.5: Speaking through Isaiah to his scattered people Israel, God tells them not to fear, promising to gather their children from east and west.
ISA.44.8: Speaking through Isaiah to Israel, God tells his people not to fear, calling them witnesses that there is no other God or Rock but him.
ISA.44.21: After mocking idols carved from firewood, God tells Israel to remember that he formed them as his servant and will never forget them.
ISA.45.3: Through Isaiah, God speaks to the Persian king Cyrus, promising him hidden treasures so he will know the God of Israel calls him by name.
ISA.49.4: In one of Isaiah's Servant songs, God's chosen servant confesses he feels his work has been wasted, yet leaves his reward with God.
ISA.50.10: Following the servant's words about enduring abuse while trusting God, the passage calls anyone walking in darkness to trust the Lord and lean on him.
ISA.63.15: In a prayer on behalf of his troubled people, Isaiah asks God to look down from heaven and asks where his zeal and compassion have gone.
JER.12.1: After learning that men of his own hometown were plotting to kill him, Jeremiah asks God why the wicked seem to prosper.
JER.15.18: Rejected and cursed by his own people for speaking God's word, Jeremiah cries out that his pain feels endless and God seems like a dry stream.
JER.20.7: After a priest had him beaten and put in the stocks, Jeremiah complains to God that answering his call has made him a laughingstock.
JER.8.18: Watching his people head toward disaster, Jeremiah pours out his grief, saying his sorrow is beyond comfort and his heart is faint.
JER.14.9: During a severe drought in Judah, Jeremiah prays for the people, asking why God seems helpless and pleading with him not to leave them.
JER.14.19: As drought, sword and famine strike Judah, Jeremiah prays for the people, asking whether God has rejected them completely.
JER.17.17: Mocked by people who scoff at his warnings, Jeremiah asks God not to become a terror to him, calling God his refuge in disaster.
JER.30.10: In a message about bringing his people home from captivity, God tells Israel through Jeremiah not to be afraid, for he will save them.
JER.31.20: In Jeremiah's message of restoration, God speaks of the northern tribes as Ephraim, his dear son whom he still remembers with deep compassion.
JER.3.12: In the days of King Josiah, God sends Jeremiah to call northern Israel, long since exiled, to come back, promising mercy instead of anger.
JER.50.20: In a prophecy against Babylon, God promises through Jeremiah that when his people return, the sins of Israel and Judah will be forgiven.
JER.29.7: In a letter to the exiles taken to Babylon, Jeremiah tells them to seek the good of that city and pray for it, since their welfare is tied to it.
LAM.1.12: The writer of Lamentations gives voice to fallen Jerusalem, pictured as a grieving woman asking passersby whether any sorrow is like hers.
LAM.2.19: Mourning Jerusalem's fall, the writer of Lamentations urges the city to cry out through the night for its starving children.
LAM.3.17: Speaking as a man who has endured God's discipline, the writer of Lamentations says he has lost all peace and forgotten what good feels like.
LAM.3.18: Describing his long ordeal after Jerusalem's fall, the writer of Lamentations admits he felt his strength and hope from the Lord were gone.
LAM.3.8: Describing the suffering of Jerusalem's fall as his own, the writer of Lamentations says that even when he cries for help, God shuts out his prayer.
EZK.18.22: Answering exiles who say they are punished for their parents' sins, God tells Ezekiel that a wicked person who turns away will have past sins forgotten.
EZK.18.31: Closing his answer to the exiles' complaint that God is unfair, God urges Israel through Ezekiel to throw off their sins and get a new heart.
EZK.33.11: When the exiles despair that their sins are wasting them away, God tells Ezekiel to say he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
EZK.34.12: After condemning Israel's selfish leaders as bad shepherds, God tells Ezekiel he himself will search for his scattered sheep and rescue them.
EZK.34.31: Closing his promise to shepherd his people himself, God tells Ezekiel's hearers that they are his flock and he is their God.
EZK.37.3: In a vision, God sets Ezekiel down in a valley full of dry bones and asks whether they can live, and Ezekiel replies that only God knows.
EZK.16.6: In Ezekiel's picture of Jerusalem as an abandoned newborn left in a field, God recalls passing by and commanding the helpless baby to live.
EZK.2.6: Commissioning Ezekiel as a prophet to rebellious Israel, God tells him three times not to fear the people or their words.
DAN.2.23: After God reveals King Nebuchadnezzar's dream to him in a night vision, Daniel thanks the God of his ancestors for wisdom and power.
DAN.9.19: Having read Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years of exile, Daniel ends his prayer of confession by begging God to forgive and act quickly.
DAN.10.11: After Daniel mourns three weeks and sees a vision by the Tigris River, a heavenly messenger calls him greatly loved and tells him to stand.
HOS.3.1: God tells the prophet Hosea to love his unfaithful wife again, as a picture of his own love for Israel as they turn to other gods.
HOS.11.1: Through Hosea, God recalls loving Israel like a young son and calling the nation out of slavery in Egypt.
HOS.11.3: Through Hosea, God recalls tenderly teaching Ephraim, the northern tribes of Israel, to walk like a small child, though they never saw his care.
HOS.11.9: After describing how his heart recoils at destroying his rebellious people, God declares through Hosea that he will not act in fierce anger.
HOS.12.6: Recalling how their ancestor Jacob wrestled and sought God, Hosea urges Israel to return to God, hold to love and justice, and wait for him.
HOS.14.1: In the closing chapter of his book, Hosea calls the people of Israel to return to God, because their sins have made them stumble.
HOS.14.2: Hosea tells Israel to come back to God bringing words of confession, and gives them a prayer asking God to remove their guilt.
HOS.14.3: In the prayer Hosea gives Israel, the people promise to stop trusting Assyria, warhorses and idols, because God shows mercy to the fatherless.
JOL.2.21: After a devastating locust plague, Joel tells the stricken land not to fear, because God is about to do great things for it.
JOL.2.23: Speaking to the people of Zion after the locust plague, Joel tells them to rejoice, for God is sending the autumn and spring rains again.
JOL.3.16: In Joel's vision of God judging the nations, the Lord roars from Jerusalem, shaking heaven and earth, while sheltering his own people.
JOL.2.14: Calling Judah to repent after a locust plague, Joel says God might yet turn back and leave a blessing, so they can offer grain and wine to him.
AMO.5.4: In a lament over the northern kingdom of Israel, Amos passes on God's message to its people to seek him and live.
AMO.7.14: When Amaziah, the priest at Bethel, orders him to go home to Judah, Amos replies that he was a herdsman and fig farmer, not a professional prophet.
JON.2.3: Praying from inside the great fish, Jonah recalls being thrown into the sea as the current swirled and the waves swept over him.
JON.2.4: Still inside the fish, Jonah admits he felt cast out of God's sight, yet says he will look again toward God's holy temple.
JON.2.6: Continuing his prayer from the fish's belly, Jonah recalls sinking to the roots of the mountains before God brought his life up from the pit.
JON.4.11: After Jonah grieves over a shade plant that withered, God asks him whether he should not care even more about the people of Nineveh.
MIC.7.9: Speaking for his humbled people to a gloating enemy, Micah says they will bear God's anger for their sin until God brings them into light.
MIC.4.5: After describing a future when nations stream to God's temple to learn his ways, Micah says his people will walk with the Lord forever.
MIC.4.6: Through Micah, God promises that a day is coming when he will gather the lame, the scattered and the hurting of his people.
MIC.5.2: Through Micah, God tells the small town of Bethlehem that a ruler over Israel, whose origins are from ancient times, will come from it.
NAM.1.13: Announcing Nineveh's coming fall, Nahum passes on God's promise to Judah that he will break Assyria's yoke from their neck.
HAB.1.3: Watching violence and injustice spread in Judah, the prophet Habakkuk asks God why he makes him see wrongdoing and seems to allow it.
HAB.1.13: After God says he will use the ruthless Babylonians to punish Judah, Habakkuk asks how a holy God can stay silent while they devour others.
HAB.2.1: Having raised his hard questions, Habakkuk says he will take his post on the watchtower and wait to hear how God will answer him.
HAB.2.20: After God's warnings against those who trust in lifeless idols, Habakkuk hears him declare that the Lord is in his holy temple and the whole earth should fall silent.
HAB.3.2: Opening his closing prayer, Habakkuk tells God he has heard of his mighty deeds and asks him to act again in their own day, and to remember mercy.
ZEP.3.15: Calling Jerusalem to sing after the judgment is past, Zephaniah announces that God has removed their punishment and now lives among them as their King.
ZEP.3.16: Looking ahead to Jerusalem's restoration, Zephaniah says the city will be told not to fear and not to let its hands hang limp.
ZEP.3.18: In Zephaniah's closing promises for Jerusalem, God says he will gather those who grieve over the appointed feasts and take away their shame.
ZEP.3.13: After warning of judgment, Zephaniah describes the humble remnant God will leave in Jerusalem, who will live honestly and rest with no one to frighten them.
HAG.1.5: Speaking to people living in paneled houses while the temple still lay in ruins, Haggai tells them God wants them to think carefully about their ways.
HAG.1.13: Once Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua and the people obey God's call to rebuild the temple, the prophet Haggai brings them this short promise from God.
ZEC.3.4: In Zechariah's vision of the high priest Joshua standing in filthy clothes, the angel of the Lord orders them removed and promises him clean, splendid robes.
ZEC.8.13: Encouraging the returned exiles as they rebuild, Zechariah tells Judah and Israel that God will turn them from a curse among the nations into a blessing.
ZEC.9.12: Right after announcing a humble king coming to Jerusalem, Zechariah calls those still held captive 'prisoners of hope' and promises them a double restoration.
ZEC.13.1: Speaking of a coming day, Zechariah announces that a fountain will be opened for David's royal house and the people of Jerusalem to wash away sin.
ZEC.7.9: When people ask whether they should keep up their mourning fasts, Zechariah reminds them of what God had told the earlier prophets about justice and mercy.
ZEC.2.5: In Zechariah's vision of a man going to measure Jerusalem, an angel passes on God's promise to be a wall of fire around the unwalled city and its glory within.
ZEC.8.19: Answering a question about the mourning fasts kept through the years of exile, God tells Zechariah those sad fasts will one day become joyful feasts for Judah.
MAL.2.10: Confronting the people of Judah for breaking faith with one another, Malachi asks whether they do not all share one Father and one Creator.
MAL.3.3: Malachi describes the Lord who will suddenly come to his temple, sitting like a refiner of silver to purify the priests, the sons of Levi.
MRK.1.35: After a long evening of healing crowds in Capernaum, Jesus gets up before dawn and goes off alone to pray.
MRK.1.11: As Jesus comes up out of the Jordan River after John baptizes him, a voice from heaven speaks over him.
MRK.1.40: A man with leprosy comes to Jesus in Galilee, kneels, and begs to be healed, saying Jesus can do it if he is willing.
MRK.2.14: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees the tax collector Levi at his booth and calls him to follow, and Levi gets up and goes.
MRK.2.27: When the Pharisees object to his disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus answers them that the Sabbath was made for people.
MRK.5.19: After Jesus frees a man from many demons near the Sea of Galilee, the man begs to come along, but Jesus sends him home to tell his own people instead.
MRK.5.28: A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years presses through the crowd around Jesus, telling herself that just touching his clothes will heal her.
MRK.5.33: When Jesus stops and asks who touched his clothes, the woman who has just been healed of her bleeding comes forward, trembling, and tells him everything.
MRK.5.41: At the house of Jairus, a synagogue leader whose twelve-year-old daughter has died, Jesus takes the girl by the hand and tells her to get up.
MRK.6.7: After being rejected in his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus calls his twelve disciples together and sends them out in pairs for the first time.
MRK.7.37: After Jesus heals a deaf man who could hardly speak, the crowds in the Decapolis region are overwhelmed with amazement at what he has done.

DEU.32.11: Continuing the song he teaches Israel before his death, Moses compares God's care for his people in the wilderness to an eagle with its young.
EPH.5.17: Urging the believers in Ephesus to live wisely and make the most of their time in evil days, Paul tells them to seek to understand the Lord's will.
JOS.14.8: At 85, Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal and recalls the day he spied out Canaan forty-five years earlier and brought back an honest report.
JOS.14.12: Reminding Joshua that God has kept him as strong as the day Moses sent him out, Caleb claims the hill country Moses promised him, where the feared Anakim live.
JOS.21.44: After Canaan is divided among the tribes and the Levites receive their towns, the narrator looks back over what God has done for Israel.
JOS.22.5: Sending the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh home across the Jordan after years of fighting beside their brothers, Joshua gives them a parting charge.
JOS.24.13: Gathering the tribes at Shechem near the end of his life, Joshua retells Israel's history in God's own voice, ending with the land they now enjoy.
JDG.3.9: After Israel turns to other gods and suffers eight years under a king of Aram, the people cry out, and God raises up the first judge, Othniel.
JDG.4.14: With Sisera's nine hundred iron chariots gathered at the Kishon River, the prophet Deborah tells Barak, waiting on Mount Tabor, that the day has come.
JDG.7.15: Creeping to the edge of the vast Midianite camp at night, Gideon overhears a man telling a dream that his friend says means Gideon will win.
JDG.8.4: After routing the Midianite army, Gideon and his three hundred men chase the fleeing kings Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan.
JDG.13.8: After an angel tells his wife she will bear a son who will begin freeing Israel from the Philistines, Manoah prays for the visitor to return and teach them.
JDG.13.23: When the angel vanishes in the altar flame, Manoah fears he and his wife will die for seeing God, and his wife, soon to be Samson's mother, reasons with him.
RUT.1.8: Widowed and setting out from Moab for home in Judah, Naomi urges her two widowed daughters-in-law, Ruth and Orpah, to go back to their mothers.
RUT.2.3: Newly arrived in Bethlehem with Naomi and no means of support, Ruth goes out to glean the leftover grain behind the harvesters.
RUT.2.11: When Ruth, bowing low in his field, asks why he would take notice of a foreigner like her, Boaz explains what he has heard about her.
RUT.2.13: After Boaz blesses her for taking refuge under God's wings, Ruth, a Moabite widow gleaning in his field, thanks him for speaking so kindly to her.
RUT.2.20: When Ruth comes home with a large amount of barley and says she worked in Boaz's field, Naomi recognizes the name and bursts out in blessing.
1SA.1.8: On the family's yearly visit to Shiloh, Hannah, childless and taunted by her rival Peninnah, weeps and will not eat, and her husband Elkanah tries to comfort her.
1SA.1.17: At the house of the Lord in Shiloh, after Hannah tells him she has been praying out of deep anguish, not drunkenness, the priest Eli answers her.
1SA.12.20: After God sends thunder and rain at wheat harvest, the frightened Israelites admit they sinned by demanding a king, and Samuel answers them.
1SA.12.23: When the Israelites, having just asked for a king, beg Samuel to pray for them, the aging prophet tells them what he will keep doing for them.
1SA.20.42: After Jonathan's arrow signal confirms that King Saul means to kill David, the two friends weep together in the field before David flees.
1SA.24.19: After David spares his life in a cave near En Gedi, cutting off only a corner of his robe, King Saul weeps and speaks to David.
1SA.26.21: After David slips into Saul's camp at night and takes the king's spear and water jug instead of killing him, Saul calls across to him.
2SA.1.23: Hearing that Saul and Jonathan have died in battle on Mount Gilboa, David composes a lament honoring both the king who hunted him and his friend.
2SA.7.28: Sitting before the Lord after the prophet Nathan brings God's promise of a lasting dynasty, David nears the end of his prayer of thanks.
2SA.9.13: The account of David's kindness to Mephibosheth, the lame son of his friend Jonathan, closes by telling where Mephibosheth now lives and eats.
1KI.4.25: Describing the height of Solomon's reign, when he ruled in peace from the Euphrates to Egypt's border, the narrator pictures ordinary life across the land.
1KI.8.50: Dedicating the temple, Solomon looks ahead to a day when Israel might sin and be carried into exile, and asks God to forgive them even there.
1KI.8.57: Rising from his knees before the altar after his dedication prayer, Solomon stands and blesses the whole assembly of Israel aloud.
1KI.8.66: After two weeks of feasting to dedicate the new temple in Jerusalem, Solomon sends the great crowd of Israelites home.
1KI.19.8: Fleeing Queen Jezebel and twice woken by an angel with bread and water in the wilderness, the exhausted prophet Elijah rises for the journey ahead.
1KI.19.18: At Mount Horeb, Elijah insists he is the only faithful prophet left in Israel, and God sends him back with new tasks and this news.
2KI.2.14: Moments after Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elisha stands alone at the Jordan holding his master's fallen cloak.
2KI.4.7: A prophet's widow, about to lose her two sons to a creditor as slaves, follows Elisha's word and fills borrowed jars with oil until none are left.
2KI.7.9: During a starving siege of Samaria, four lepers find the Aramean camp abandoned, and after feasting and hiding plunder, they stop themselves.
1CH.5.20: In a record of the tribes east of the Jordan, the chronicler notes how Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh fared in their war with the Hagrites.
1CH.14.10: Soon after David is anointed king over all Israel, the Philistines raid the Valley of Rephaim, and before going out to face them, David asks God.
1CH.21.24: To stop a plague sent after his census, David goes to buy Ornan's threshing floor for an altar, and Ornan offers to give him everything free.
1CH.22.9: Charging his young son Solomon to build the temple, David repeats what God told him: that a man of war could not build it, but his son would.
1CH.23.30: As David organizes the Levites for service in the future temple in Jerusalem, the chronicler lists their duties, including this daily one.
1CH.28.20: Handing over detailed plans for the temple, David charges his son Solomon before Israel's leaders to see the great work through.
2CH.15.4: Returning from victory over a vast Cushite army, King Asa is met by the prophet Azariah, who recalls how Israel found God in times of trouble.
2CH.15.15: Stirred by Azariah's prophecy, King Asa gathers Judah in Jerusalem, where the people swear with shouts and trumpets to seek the Lord.
2CH.20.20: On the morning they march out toward the invading armies of Moab and Ammon, King Jehoshaphat stops to address the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
2CH.25.9: King Amaziah of Judah has paid a hundred talents to hire soldiers from Israel when a man of God warns him to send them home before the battle.
2CH.36.15: Near the end of Judah's story, as King Zedekiah, the priests and the people grow ever more unfaithful, the chronicler notes how God kept reaching out to them.
EZR.3.13: At the laying of the second temple's foundation in Jerusalem, the loud weeping of those who remembered the first temple mixes with shouts of joy.
EZR.5.5: When the Persian governor Tattenai demands to know who authorized the Jews to rebuild the temple, the builders keep working while he writes to King Darius.
EZR.6.22: With the rebuilt temple finally finished, the returned exiles celebrate Passover and the week of Unleavened Bread in Jerusalem.
EZR.8.21: Camped by the Ahava Canal with families preparing to return from Babylon to Jerusalem, Ezra faces a long road with no royal escort.
EZR.8.31: After fasting and praying at the Ahava Canal, Ezra and the returning exiles set out for Jerusalem carrying silver, gold and temple treasures.
NEH.2.4: Serving wine to King Artaxerxes, Nehemiah is asked what he wants, and he sends up a silent prayer in the moment before he answers.
NEH.2.18: After secretly inspecting Jerusalem's broken walls by night, Nehemiah gathers the city's leaders and calls them to rebuild.
NEH.4.6: Mocked by Sanballat and by Tobiah, who jeers that even a fox could knock their wall down, Nehemiah and the builders keep working on Jerusalem's wall.
NEH.4.9: When Sanballat, Tobiah and their allies plot to attack Jerusalem and stop the rebuilding, Nehemiah and the builders respond in two ways.
NEH.8.8: As Ezra reads the Law aloud from a wooden platform to the crowd gathered in Jerusalem, Levites help the people understand what they hear.
NEH.9.21: In a long prayer of confession, the Levites recall how God kept caring for Israel through the wilderness, even after the golden calf.
EST.4.4: When Queen Esther, not yet knowing of Haman's decree against the Jews, hears that her cousin Mordecai is mourning in sackcloth, she is deeply distressed.
EST.6.1: On the night before Haman plans to ask for Mordecai's hanging, King Xerxes cannot sleep and calls for the royal records to be read to him.
EST.6.3: Hearing from the royal records that Mordecai once exposed a plot to assassinate him, King Xerxes asks how he was rewarded.
EST.8.6: Though Haman has been hanged, his decree to destroy the Jews still stands, so Queen Esther falls weeping at King Xerxes' feet to plead again.
JOB.2.13: When Job's friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar arrive and can barely recognize him, they weep, tear their robes and sit down with him.
JOB.6.10: Answering his friend Eliphaz, the suffering Job wishes God would end his life, and names the one comfort he still has in his pain.
JOB.6.11: Told by Eliphaz that his piety and integrity should give him hope, Job, sick and stripped of everything, pushes back from the depths of his pain.
JOB.7.4: Still replying to Eliphaz, Job describes his sleepless nights, lying down only to wish for morning while he tosses until dawn.
JOB.7.6: Worn down by sickness and loss, Job says his days are racing past like a weaver's shuttle and running out with no hope in sight.
JOB.8.7: Bildad, one of Job's friends, promises that if Job turns to God his future will far outstrip his past; God does later restore Job's fortunes.
JOB.10.1: After Bildad insists that God never rejects the innocent, Job refuses to stay quiet and decides to pour out his bitterness to God.
JOB.12.13: Answering his friend Zophar's lecture, Job agrees that God is wise and powerful, and insists he knows it as well as any of them.
JOB.13.24: Turning from his friends to speak to God directly, Job asks why God has gone silent and seems to treat him as an enemy.
JOB.14.17: Wondering whether a person who dies can live again, Job pictures a day when God would call him back and seal his wrongdoing away.
JOB.17.9: Mocked and grieving, and with his friends offering no comfort, Job still declares that people who do right keep going and grow stronger.
JOB.19.7: Answering Bildad's second speech, Job complains that he cries out that he has been wronged, yet no one answers him and no justice comes.
JOB.19.26: Moments after declaring that his Redeemer lives, Job adds that even after his body is destroyed, he will see God with his own eyes.
JOB.30.27: In his final defense, Job sets his old life of honor beside his present misery and says he is churning inside and cannot rest.
JOB.30.31: Ending his final defense, Job sets the honored, joyful life he once had beside the fever, loneliness and scorn that fill his days now.
JOB.33.28: Elihu, a younger man who speaks after Job's friends fall silent, describes someone God spares from death, who then tells others of his rescue.
JOB.34.32: Elihu, the young man who breaks into Job's debate with his friends, suggests the humble words a person should say to God after doing wrong.
JOB.37.14: After describing God's power in storms, rain and ice, Elihu urges Job to stop and consider God's wonders, just before God himself speaks.
JOB.42.6: Having heard God speak to him out of the whirlwind, Job ends his reply by taking back his earlier words and repenting in dust and ashes.
PRO.1.33: Solomon pictures Wisdom as a woman calling out in the streets; after warning those who ignore her, she promises safety to anyone who listens.
PRO.3.28: Teaching his son how to treat the people around him, Solomon warns against putting off a neighbor in need when help is already at hand.
PRO.10.19: In one of his short paired sayings about speech, Solomon observes that the more a person talks, the more likely they are to do wrong.
PRO.12.20: In this proverb, Solomon contrasts people who plot harm with people who counsel peace, and says it is the peacemakers who end up with joy.
PRO.14.29: Among Solomon's sayings about self-control, this one sets a patient, slow-to-anger person against someone whose quick temper leads to folly.
PRO.16.6: In a run of sayings about the Lord's rule over people's plans and hearts, Solomon pairs mercy and faithfulness with the fear of God.
PRO.17.1: Solomon, reflecting on home life, says a simple meal eaten in peace is better than a feast in a house full of quarrels.
PRO.17.3: Solomon compares the way fire refines silver and gold to the way God tests and examines the human heart.
PRO.17.27: Among Solomon's sayings about speech, this one says a person who truly understands knows when to hold back words and stays calm.
PRO.20.5: Solomon pictures a person's real intentions as deep water, hidden below the surface, which a wise and understanding person knows how to draw out.
PRO.25.20: In the sayings of Solomon copied by King Hezekiah's scribes, this proverb warns that singing cheerful songs to a grieving person only hurts.
PRO.25.28: Another of Solomon's sayings copied by King Hezekiah's scribes compares a person with no self-control to a city whose walls are broken down.
PRO.26.20: In a string of Solomon's sayings copied by King Hezekiah's scribes about quarrels, this one says conflict dies down once gossip stops.
PRO.27.5: In the collection of Solomon's sayings copied by King Hezekiah's scribes, this proverb values honest correction over love that is never shown.
PRO.27.10: From Solomon's sayings copied by King Hezekiah's scribes, this one urges keeping old friends, since a neighbor close by helps most in a crisis.
PRO.27.19: Among the proverbs King Hezekiah's scribes collected from Solomon, this saying sits beside one about iron sharpening iron and friends shaping each other.
ECC.1.8: Surveying the endless cycles of sun, wind and rivers, the Preacher says everything is wearisome and people are never satisfied by what they see.
ECC.1.4: Opening his reflections, the Preacher notes that whole generations come and go while the earth itself stays, asking what anyone's labor gains.
ECC.2.17: Realizing that the wise and the foolish die alike and are both forgotten, the Preacher admits that for a time he hated life itself.
ECC.5.2: Giving advice about going to the house of God, the Preacher warns against rushing into words before God, since God is in heaven.
ECC.5.20: Having called the ability to enjoy one's work a gift from God, the Preacher says such a person is kept too busy with gladness to brood.
ECC.7.1: Opening a set of sayings about death and mourning, the Preacher values a good name over fine perfume and a life's end over its beginning.
ECC.7.13: Just before advising how to face good days and bad ones, the Preacher asks his readers to consider God's work and what no one can undo.
ECC.9.4: After observing that the same fate comes to everyone, the Preacher says there is still hope for the living: even a live dog beats a dead lion.
ECC.9.9: Urging his readers to enjoy life while they can, the Preacher tells a man to delight in his wife through all the short days God gives him.
ECC.9.17: After telling of a poor wise man who saved his city but was soon forgotten, the Preacher says quiet wise words matter more than a ruler's shouts.
ECC.11.4: Near the end of the book, the Preacher warns that anyone who waits for perfect wind and weather will never get around to sowing or reaping.
ECC.11.10: Speaking to a young man, the Preacher urges him to put away sorrow and pain, because the days of youth and strength do not last.
SNG.2.3: In this love poem attributed to Solomon, the young woman answers her beloved's praise by saying he stands out among young men like an apple tree.
SNG.2.10: Watching her beloved arrive and gaze through the lattice, the young woman hears him call her his beautiful one and invite her to come away.
SNG.2.12: Continuing his invitation to his beloved, the young man points to the flowers, the songbirds and the cooing doves as signs that spring has come.
SNG.2.14: The young man calls to his beloved as a dove hidden in the clefts of the rock, longing to see her face and hear her voice.
JHN.15.10: On the night before his death, using the picture of a vine and its branches, Jesus tells his disciples that keeping his commands keeps them in his love.
SNG.4.9: Praising his bride in this love poem, the groom tells her she has captured his heart with a single glance of her eyes.
SNG.4.12: In the same song of praise, the groom pictures his bride as a locked garden and a sealed spring, a beauty kept for him alone.
SNG.5.16: Asked by the women of Jerusalem what makes her beloved special, the young woman describes him from head to toe and ends by calling him her friend.
PSA.4.3: Speaking to people who have been dragging his name through the mud, David tells them that God has set apart the faithful and hears his prayers.
PSA.6.4: Sick, frail and deeply troubled, David pleads with God to turn back toward him and rescue him, appealing to God's steadfast love.
PSA.17.15: Closing a prayer for protection from ruthless enemies, David contrasts people whose reward is in this life with his own hope of seeing God's face.
PSA.25.8: Right after asking God to forget the sins of his youth, David says that because God is good and upright, he shows wrongdoers the right way.
PSA.25.14: Continuing his prayer for guidance and forgiveness, David says God shares his friendship and his covenant with those who fear him.
PSA.27.9: Having told God that he will seek his face, David pleads with God not to hide from him or turn him away, since God has always been his help.
PSA.30.3: In a thanksgiving psalm headed for the dedication of the temple, David praises God for pulling him back from the brink of death.
PSA.30.7: David admits that when life went well he felt he could never be shaken, but when God seemed to hide his face, he was suddenly terrified.
PSA.31.12: Shunned by neighbors and avoided by his own friends, David says he feels forgotten like someone long dead, like a broken clay pot.
PSA.31.21: After describing enemies plotting against his life, David breaks into praise for the love God showed him when he was hemmed in like a city under siege.
PSA.32.4: Describing the time before he confessed his sin, David says God's hand weighed on him day and night, draining his strength like summer heat.
PSA.33.11: In this hymn with no named author, the psalm's writer contrasts the failed schemes of nations with God's plans, which stand forever.
PSA.34.7: In the psalm David wrote after escaping a Philistine king by pretending to be insane, he pictures God's angel camped around those who fear God.
PSA.35.17: Attacked by people he had once prayed and fasted for when they were sick, David asks God how long he will simply stand by and watch.
PSA.37.6: Urging readers to trust God rather than envy people who prosper by doing wrong, David says the Lord will make their integrity shine like the dawn.
PSA.38.3: In a psalm written 'for remembrance,' David, sick and weighed down by guilt, tells God that his whole body is in pain because of his sin.
PSA.39.6: Troubled by how brief life is, David pictures people rushing about like shadows, piling up wealth without knowing who will end up with it.
PSA.40.12: Shortly after thanking God for a past rescue, David finds himself surrounded by troubles again and overwhelmed by the weight of his own sins.
PSA.42.2: In this psalm of the sons of Korah, a writer far from the temple longs for the day he can come and stand in God's presence again.
PSA.42.7: Remembering God from far away, near the Jordan and Mount Hermon, the writer of this psalm feels sorrow crashing over him like deep waters.
PSA.44.22: In a lament by the sons of Korah, the nation protests it has stayed loyal to God yet suffers anyway, a line Paul later quotes in Romans.
PSA.51.4: Pleading for mercy after Nathan exposed his adultery with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, David faces God with the full truth of what he has done.
PSA.51.6: In his prayer of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba, David says God wants honesty deep inside a person, and asks God to teach him wisdom there.
PSA.51.8: Crushed by guilt after Nathan exposed his sin with Bathsheba, David asks God to let him hear joy again and make his broken bones rejoice.
PSA.55.12: Surrounded by violence in the city, David says what hurts most is that the one attacking him is not an enemy but a close friend.
PSA.62.10: Having called God his only rock and refuge, David warns his listeners not to trust in extortion or set their hearts on growing wealth.
PSA.66.12: In this thanksgiving psalm with no named author, the writer looks back on the hard trials God's people went through and where God brought them.
PSA.66.18: Telling others what God has done for him, the writer of this thanksgiving psalm admits that God would not have listened if he had held on to sin.
PSA.68.6: In a psalm celebrating God as a father to the fatherless, David adds that God gives lonely people a family and leads prisoners into freedom.
PSA.69.2: Hated without cause by many enemies, David describes himself sinking in deep mud with no footing, as floodwaters close over him.
2CO.4.1: After contrasting the fading glory on Moses' face with the new covenant's lasting glory, Paul tells the Corinthians how he views his ministry.
PSA.71.21: Looking back on many troubles in a long life, the aging writer of this psalm trusts God to restore his honor and comfort him again.
ROM.11.32: Ending his long reflection on Israel and the Gentiles, Paul concludes that God's purpose behind everyone's disobedience is mercy for all.
PSA.77.3: In a sleepless time of trouble, Asaph admits that even thinking about God, which should have comforted him, only made him groan.
PSA.80.4: In a prayer for a nation in ruins, Asaph asks the God of Israel how long he will stay angry even while his people keep praying.
PSA.85.4: After recalling how God once forgave his people and restored the land, the sons of Korah ask God to restore them again and set aside his anger.
PSA.86.3: In a prayer where he calls himself poor and needy, David asks God to be merciful to him, since he calls out to God all day long.
PSA.88.9: In this bleak psalm of the sons of Korah, credited to Heman the Ezrahite, the writer tells God his eyes are dim with grief as he calls out every day.
PSA.88.12: Feeling close to death in one of the darkest psalms, Heman asks God whether his wonders and goodness can be known in the grave.
PSA.90.10: Moses, in the psalm credited to him, weighs the short span of a human life, seventy or eighty years, against God's everlasting existence.
PSA.90.13: After asking God to teach his people to number their days, Moses pleads with God to return and have compassion on his servants.
PSA.90.15: Near the end of his prayer about life's brevity, Moses asks God to give his people as many years of gladness as they have had of trouble.
PSA.91.7: In this psalm about the safety of those who shelter in God, the psalm's writer promises that disaster may strike thousands nearby yet not reach them.
PSA.94.9: Answering people who crush the weak while claiming that God does not see, the psalm's writer asks whether the one who made the eye cannot see.
PSA.95.1: With no named author, this psalm opens by calling God's people to gather and sing loudly to God, the rock who saves them.
PSA.102.4: In a prayer headed as the lament of an afflicted person growing faint, the psalm's writer says his heart has withered so much he forgets to eat.
PSA.103.19: After contrasting fleeting human lives with God's everlasting love, David declares that God's throne is set in heaven and he rules over all.
PSA.113.9: Closing a short hymn about a God who lifts up the lowly, the psalm's writer praises him for giving a childless woman a home full of children.
PSA.116.3: Looking back on a time he nearly died, the psalm's writer describes being caught in death's ropes and overwhelmed by trouble and sorrow.
PSA.118.13: In a festival psalm of thanks, the writer recalls being surrounded by hostile nations and pushed to the point of falling before the Lord helped him.
PSA.119.9: Opening the second section of Psalm 119, a long alphabetic poem about God's word, the writer asks how a young person can keep his life pure.
PSA.119.82: Slandered by arrogant people, the writer of Psalm 119 says his eyes grow tired from watching for God's promise, and asks when comfort will come.
PSA.119.151: Rising before dawn to pray while people bent on wickedness close in around him, the writer of Psalm 119 reminds himself that God is nearer still.
PSA.121.6: In a song of ascents for pilgrims traveling up to Jerusalem, the psalm's writer promises that neither the sun by day nor the moon by night will harm them.
ISA.54.14: Speaking to Jerusalem as a forsaken wife God will rebuild with precious stones, Isaiah promises her a future far from oppression and terror.
ROM.8.25: Writing to believers in Rome about a creation groaning for redemption, Paul says hope is for what is not yet seen, so they wait for it patiently.
PSA.139.8: Asking where he could possibly go to escape God's presence, David pictures both the heights of heaven and the depths of the grave.
PSA.142.2: Hiding in a cave while King Saul hunts him, David cries aloud to the Lord for mercy, feeling that no one else cares whether he lives.
ISA.1.17: Rejecting Judah's festivals and prayers raised by blood-stained hands, God tells the people through Isaiah to learn to do right and defend the weak.
ISA.6.7: In Isaiah's vision of God in the temple, a seraph touches the prophet's lips with a burning coal from the altar and declares his guilt removed.
ISA.8.17: As Assyria threatens and God seems to hide his face from Israel, Isaiah resolves to wait for the Lord and keep trusting him.
ISA.9.7: Right after naming the child who will be called Prince of Peace, Isaiah says the peace of his reign on David's throne will never stop growing.
ISA.12.5: In the short song Isaiah gives the people for the day God's anger turns to comfort, they are told to sing of his glorious deeds to the whole earth.
ISA.48.18: Speaking through Isaiah as the Redeemer who teaches his people, God laments that Israel did not listen, since their peace could have flowed like a river.
ISA.50.4: In one of Isaiah's songs about the Servant of the Lord, the Servant says God wakes him each morning to listen, so he can sustain the weary with a word.
ISA.52.12: Calling the exiles to leave Babylon, Isaiah tells them they will not flee in haste as from Egypt, for God will go before them and guard them from behind.
ISA.54.9: Speaking to Jerusalem as a forsaken wife called back home, God recalls his oath after Noah's flood and swears in the same way not to be angry with her again.
ISA.57.2: Grieving that the righteous die and no one takes it to heart, Isaiah says the upright are spared the evil to come and find peace and rest in death.
ISA.57.16: Right after saying he dwells with the humble and contrite, God says through Isaiah that he will not stay angry forever, or the human spirit would fail.
ISA.62.5: Picturing restored Jerusalem as a bride reunited with her land and her people, Isaiah says God will rejoice over her like a bridegroom.
ISA.63.16: Praying for his people after recalling how God once led them through the sea, Isaiah insists God is still their Father even if Abraham would not recognize them.
ISA.64.6: In a prayer of confession for a nation that has sinned, Isaiah admits that even their best deeds are stained and their sins are sweeping them away like wind.
ISA.64.12: Ending a long prayer over a burned temple and a ruined Jerusalem, Isaiah asks whether God will stay silent and keep afflicting his people.
JER.1.7: When the young Jeremiah protests that he is only a child and cannot speak, God tells him not to say that, but to go wherever he is sent.
JER.2.13: Through Jeremiah, God accuses his people of trading him for worthless idols, abandoning a spring of living water for cracked cisterns they dug themselves.
JER.8.20: As enemy armies sweep toward Judah, Jeremiah hears his people cry that the harvest and the summer have both passed and still no rescue has come.
JER.12.5: When Jeremiah complains that the wicked prosper, God answers bluntly that if racing men has worn him out, harder contests with horses still lie ahead.
JER.14.8: Praying for Judah during a severe drought, Jeremiah calls God the hope of Israel and asks why he seems like a stranger passing through for a single night.
JER.20.9: Beaten and put in the stocks for his message, Jeremiah says that whenever he tries to stay silent, God's word burns like fire shut up in his bones.
JER.31.33: In his promise of a new covenant to replace the one broken after Egypt, God says through Jeremiah that he will write his law on his people's hearts.
LAM.2.13: Watching children faint in the streets of fallen Jerusalem, the writer of Lamentations searches for words to console a city whose wound is deep as the sea.
LAM.3.1: Opening the central poem of Lamentations, the writer speaks as a man who has personally suffered under God's discipline in Jerusalem's fall.
LAM.3.25: Having called God's mercies new every morning, the writer of Lamentations goes on to say that the Lord is good to those who wait for him.
LAM.3.27: Still searching for hope amid Jerusalem's ruins, the writer of Lamentations says it is good for a person to learn to carry the yoke while still young.
LAM.3.38: Wrestling honestly with the disaster that fell on Jerusalem, the writer of Lamentations asks whether both hardship and good come from God's own mouth.
LAM.3.42: Having urged his people to lift their hearts to God, the writer of Lamentations voices their confession of rebellion and their sense of no pardon yet.
LAM.3.44: At the lowest point of his lament over Jerusalem, the writer of Lamentations tells God it feels as if a cloud blocks every prayer from reaching him.
LAM.5.16: In the closing prayer of Lamentations, the survivors of Jerusalem's fall mourn their lost joy and glory, confessing that their own sin brought them low.
EZK.16.60: After a long picture of Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife, God tells Ezekiel he will still remember his covenant with her and make one that lasts forever.
EZK.22.30: After listing the corruption of Jerusalem's priests, officials, prophets and people, God tells Ezekiel he looked for someone to stand in the gap.
EZK.37.23: Speaking to exiles whose idol worship had led to their scattering, God promises through Ezekiel to rescue them from their sin and make them his own again.
EZK.34.15: Condemning Israel's leaders as shepherds who fed only themselves, God tells Ezekiel he will tend his flock himself and let them lie down in rich pasture.
EZK.36.9: Speaking to the mountains of Israel, left desolate and mocked by the nations, God tells Ezekiel he is on the land's side and it will be farmed again.
EZK.36.27: Promising his exiled people a new heart, God tells Ezekiel he will also put his own Spirit within them so they can walk in his ways.
EZK.37.11: After Ezekiel watches dry bones come to life in a vision, God explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say their hope is lost.
EZK.37.26: After the dry-bones vision and the joining of two sticks into one, God tells Ezekiel he will make a lasting covenant of peace with his reunited people.
DAN.1.8: Taken to Babylon as a young exile, renamed Belteshazzar and given rich food from King Nebuchadnezzar's own table, Daniel faces a quiet test of loyalty.
DAN.2.21: Facing death with Babylon's other wise men unless the king's dream is explained, Daniel receives the answer at night and praises God.
DAN.4.34: After living like an animal in the fields as God had warned, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon looks up to heaven, recovers his sanity and praises the Most High.
DAN.4.37: Restored to his throne after God humbled his pride, King Nebuchadnezzar ends his own account by praising the King of heaven.
DAN.6.23: Daniel has just called out from the den that God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths, and King Darius, after a sleepless night of fasting, hears him.
DAN.9.8: In a long prayer of confession for his exiled nation, Daniel admits that its kings, leaders and ancestors all share the shame of having sinned against God.
DAN.10.8: Standing by the Tigris River, Daniel alone sees a dazzling man dressed in linen, and as his terrified companions flee and hide, all his strength drains away.
DAN.12.13: In the final words of his book, Daniel is told by a heavenly messenger to go his way, rest, and rise to receive his inheritance at the end of days.
HOS.2.15: Picturing Israel as his unfaithful wife, God says through Hosea he will woo her in the wilderness and make the Valley of Achor, or 'Trouble,' a door of hope.
HOS.3.5: After Hosea buys back his unfaithful wife as a picture of God's love, he foretells that Israel too will one day return to seek God and David their king.
HOS.13.5: Speaking through Hosea to an Israel that now worships idols, God recalls that he has been their God ever since he brought them out of Egypt.
HOS.13.6: Grieving over Israel's idols, God traces the problem through Hosea: once the people were well fed, their hearts grew proud and they forgot him.
HOS.14.5: Answering Israel's prayer of return at the end of Hosea's book, God promises to be like refreshing dew so that his people will blossom and take root.
HOS.14.9: In the final verse of Hosea's book, the prophet invites anyone who is wise to take these words to heart, because the Lord's ways are right.
JOL.1.3: Opening his book after a locust plague unlike anything in living memory, Joel tells the elders to pass the story down to their children and grandchildren.
JOL.2.17: Calling a fast after the locust disaster, Joel tells the priests to weep at the temple and beg God to spare his people from the nations' scorn.
JOL.2.18: Once the people gather to fast and the priests weep for mercy, Joel reports that the Lord became jealous for his land and took pity on his people.
JOL.2.22: After the locust plague stripped the land bare, Joel speaks even to the wild animals, telling them not to fear because the pastures are green again.
AMO.3.3: Opening a series of everyday questions about cause and effect, Amos asks whether two can walk together without agreeing, as he warns Israel of coming judgment.
AMO.4.13: After listing disasters that failed to turn Israel back and warning them to prepare to meet their God, Amos describes the Lord who forms the mountains.
AMO.5.15: Condemning bribery and oppression of the poor in Israel's courts, Amos urges the people to hate evil and love good, in hope that God will be gracious.
AMO.7.15: Continuing his reply to the priest who ordered him out of Bethel, Amos says it was the Lord who took him from following the flock and sent him to Israel.
AMO.9.15: In the closing promise of his book, Amos foresees God restoring Israel from captivity and planting them in their land, never to be uprooted again.
OBA.1.3: Obadiah delivers God's message to Edom, a nation living high among rocky cliffs and trusting in its heights, warning that its pride has deceived it.
OBA.1.21: Obadiah ends his short prophecy against Edom by promising that deliverers will go up Mount Zion and the kingdom will belong to the Lord.
JON.2.5: From the belly of the great fish, Jonah describes sinking into the deep as the waters closed around him and seaweed wrapped around his head.
JON.2.8: Near the end of his prayer from inside the great fish, remembering how God heard him as his life ebbed away, Jonah turns to those who trust in idols.
JON.3.2: After running from his first assignment and being rescued from the sea, Jonah hears God's call a second time: go to Nineveh and proclaim his message.
JON.4.2: Angry that God spared Nineveh, Jonah admits this is why he first fled toward Tarshish: he knew God was gracious, compassionate and slow to anger.
JON.4.3: His warning of doom for Nineveh now undone by God's mercy, Jonah finishes his bitter complaint to God with a desperate request.
JON.4.4: After Jonah angrily asks to die because God spared Nineveh, the Lord replies with one quiet question for him to consider.
MIC.3.8: Condemning prophets who promise peace to anyone who feeds them, Micah declares that he himself is filled with the Spirit's power to name Israel's sin.
MIC.4.2: In a vision of the last days that Isaiah also records, Micah sees many nations streaming to the Lord's mountain in Jerusalem to learn his ways.
MIC.4.7: Continuing his promise to gather the lame and scattered, God says through Micah that these weakest ones will become a remnant and a strong nation.
MIC.6.3: Summoning the mountains as witnesses to his case against Israel, God asks his people through Micah what he has done to weary them.
MIC.6.6: After God recalls rescuing Israel from Egypt, Micah voices a worshiper's question: what offering could possibly be enough to bring before the Lord?
MIC.7.20: Micah ends his book right after marveling at a God who pardons sin, trusting him to keep the faithful love he swore to Abraham and Jacob.
NAM.1.3: Opening his message against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, Nahum describes God as slow to anger yet great in power, never leaving guilt unpunished.
NAM.1.9: Announcing Nineveh's fall, Nahum tells those who plot against the Lord that God will finish them, so the trouble they brought will not rise again.
HAB.1.4: In his opening complaint, Habakkuk tells God that violence has spread so far in Judah that the law is paralyzed and justice is twisted.
HAB.1.5: Answering Habakkuk's complaint about injustice, God says he is about to do something unbelievable: raise up the Babylonians to bring judgment.
HAB.1.12: Troubled that God would use the ruthless Babylonians to bring judgment, Habakkuk appeals to God as everlasting, his Holy One and his Rock.
HAB.2.2: After Habakkuk takes his post on the watchtower to wait for an answer, God tells him to write the vision down plainly so a messenger can run with it.
HAB.3.16: After a vision of God marching out to save his people, Habakkuk trembles to his bones, yet resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress.
ZEP.2.3: Warning Judah that the day of the Lord's anger is near, Zephaniah urges the humble of the earth to seek righteousness and humility while there is still time.
ZEP.3.11: Looking beyond judgment on Jerusalem, Zephaniah promises that the city will no longer be shamed by its past sins once God removes the proud from its midst.
ZEP.3.12: Once the proud are removed from Jerusalem, Zephaniah says, God will leave in the city a meek and lowly people who trust in his name.
ZEP.3.20: In the last line of Zephaniah's prophecy, God promises to gather his scattered people home and make them honored among all the nations.
HAG.1.6: Rebuking returned exiles who lived in fine houses while the temple lay in ruins, Haggai points out that all their hard work never leaves them satisfied.
HAG.2.3: As the returned exiles rebuild the temple, Haggai asks those old enough to remember Solomon's temple whether this new one seems like nothing by comparison.
HAG.2.8: Promising through Haggai to shake the nations and fill the unfinished temple with glory, God answers the builders' worry that their work looks poor and small.
HAG.2.23: In his last recorded message, Haggai tells Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, that God will shake the nations and overthrow kingdoms but will choose him.
ZEC.2.10: After calling the remaining exiles home from Babylon, Zechariah tells Jerusalem to sing for joy because God is coming to live among his people.
ZEC.3.2: In Zechariah's vision, Satan stands ready to accuse Joshua the high priest, and the Lord rebukes the accuser, calling Joshua a stick snatched from the fire.
ZEC.4.10: As the returned exiles lay the modest foundation of a new temple under Zerubbabel, God tells Zechariah that no one should look down on small beginnings.
ZEC.8.6: Promising that old people and playing children will again fill Jerusalem's streets, God asks through Zechariah whether what seems impossible to the remnant is impossible for him.
ZEC.9.16: After picturing God as a warrior fighting on behalf of Judah, Zechariah turns to how the Lord will treat his people once the battle is won.
ZEC.10.12: Promising to gather his scattered people back from Egypt and Assyria, God says through Zechariah that he will strengthen Judah and Ephraim to walk in his name.
ZEC.14.7: In a vision of the coming Day of the Lord, when God stands on the Mount of Olives, Zechariah describes a strange day without ordinary night, where evening brings light.
MAL.2.6: Rebuking the careless priests of his day, God through Malachi recalls his covenant with Levi and the ideal priest who taught truthfully and turned many from sin.
MAL.2.15: Confronting men of Judah who were breaking faith with their wives, Malachi urges them to guard their hearts and stay faithful to the wife of their youth.
MAL.2.17: Malachi tells the people of Judah that they have worn God out with cynical talk, including the complaint that God favors evildoers and justice is nowhere.
MAL.3.1: Answering people who ask where the God of justice is, God promises through Malachi to send a messenger ahead of him, a promise the Gospels link to John the Baptist.
MAL.3.14: Malachi records God quoting the complaint of discouraged people in Judah who say serving him has been pointless, since the arrogant seem to prosper.
MAT.6.30: Still teaching about worry in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus points from the wildflowers to the short-lived grass of the field and turns to his anxious listeners.
MAT.10.16: Sending out the twelve disciples to preach in the towns of Israel, Jesus warns them of the danger ahead and tells them how to carry themselves.
MAT.14.26: Rowing against the wind in the dark hours before dawn, the disciples see Jesus walking toward their boat across the sea and think he is a ghost.
MAT.14.33: After Jesus rescues the sinking Peter and the wind dies down, the disciples in the boat fall down and worship him.
MAT.18.3: When the disciples ask who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, Jesus calls a little child to stand among them and gives this answer.
MRK.1.15: After John the Baptist is arrested, Jesus goes into Galilee and begins his public preaching with this announcement.
MRK.2.12: In a crowded house in Capernaum, a paralyzed man lowered through the roof by his friends is told by Jesus to get up, pick up his mat and go home.
MRK.3.5: In a synagogue on the Sabbath, with critics watching to accuse him, Jesus is grieved by their hard hearts and turns to a man with a withered hand.
MRK.3.13: Pressed by crowds seeking healing near the Sea of Galilee, Jesus goes up a mountain and calls the ones he wants, the start of choosing the Twelve.
MRK.4.28: In a short parable only Mark records, Jesus compares God's kingdom to seed that a farmer scatters and that grows on its own while he sleeps.
MRK.5.30: Pressed by a crowd on the way to Jairus's house, Jesus feels healing power leave him when a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak.
MRK.5.35: While Jesus is still speaking to the woman he has just healed, messengers reach Jairus, a synagogue leader whose young daughter was dying.
MRK.6.37: Before feeding the five thousand in a remote place, Jesus tells his disciples to feed the hungry crowd themselves, and they balk at the cost.
MRK.7.33: In the Decapolis region, people bring Jesus a deaf man who can hardly speak, and he leads him away from the crowd to heal him in private.
MRK.8.2: Before feeding the four thousand, Jesus tells his disciples he is moved for a crowd that has stayed with him three days with nothing left to eat.
MRK.8.24: At Bethsaida, Jesus leads a blind man out of the village and touches his eyes, and the man describes his first, partial glimpse of sight.
MRK.8.25: After a first touch leaves the blind man of Bethsaida seeing people like walking trees, Jesus lays his hands on the man's eyes once more.
MRK.9.27: After Jesus drives a spirit out of a convulsing boy, the boy lies so still that many in the crowd say he is dead, and Jesus reaches for his hand.
MRK.10.22: A rich man who asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life is told he must sell everything, give to the poor and follow him.
MRK.10.50: Outside Jericho, the blind beggar Bartimaeus keeps shouting for Jesus though the crowd tries to hush him, and then word comes that Jesus is calling him.
MRK.10.51: When blind Bartimaeus, who has been shouting for mercy on the road out of Jericho, is brought to him, Jesus asks him a simple question.
MRK.12.17: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, and he asks them whose image is on a Roman coin.
MRK.12.34: A scribe agrees with Jesus that loving God and neighbor matters more than all burnt offerings, and Jesus responds to his thoughtful answer.
MRK.14.50: When an armed crowd sent by the chief priests arrests Jesus in Gethsemane, the disciples who had all vowed never to desert him are there with him.
MRK.16.1: After Jesus has been crucified and buried, three women who had followed him wait for the Sabbath to end so they can tend to his body.
MRK.16.8: Told by a young man in white at the empty tomb that Jesus has risen, the women hurry away, and in the earliest manuscripts Mark's Gospel ends here.
MRK.16.9: In the longer ending found in many manuscripts of Mark, the story of the resurrection is retold, beginning with Jesus' first appearance.
LUK.1.49: Still singing after Elizabeth hails her as the mother of her Lord, Mary moves from her own lowliness to what God has done for her.
LUK.2.52: After twelve-year-old Jesus is found in the temple and goes home to Nazareth with his parents, Luke sums up the years of his growing up.
LUK.9.62: On the road, one would-be follower asks Jesus to let him first say goodbye to his family, and Jesus replies with a farming image.
LUK.10.2: Appointing more followers beyond the Twelve to go ahead of him on his way toward Jerusalem, Jesus begins his instructions by describing the work.
LUK.10.21: When the followers he sent out in pairs return full of joy at what they have seen, Jesus himself rejoices and thanks the Father in prayer.
LUK.17.5: After Jesus tells them to keep forgiving a brother who wrongs them even seven times in one day, the apostles make this request.
LUK.17.17: Noticing that only one of the ten men healed of leprosy has come back to give thanks, and he a Samaritan, Jesus asks aloud about the rest.
LUK.19.8: While the crowd in Jericho grumbles that Jesus is staying with a sinner, the tax collector Zacchaeus stands up and makes Jesus a promise.
LUK.24.11: On the morning Jesus rises, Mary Magdalene, Joanna and other women tell the apostles about the empty tomb and what they were told there.
LUK.24.12: When the apostles dismiss the women's report of an empty tomb as nonsense, Peter gets up anyway and runs to see for himself.
