JHN.5.7: At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus asks a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years whether he wants to get well, and the man explains his situation.
JHN.6.9: Facing a hungry crowd of thousands, Jesus asks Philip where to buy bread, and Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, points out what little food is at hand.
JHN.6.67: After many followers walk away over his hard teaching about being the bread of life, Jesus turns to the twelve and asks them this question.
JHN.11.5: When Lazarus falls ill in Bethany and his sisters send word to Jesus, John pauses to note how Jesus felt about this family.
JHN.12.3: At a dinner in Bethany six days before Passover, with Lazarus at the table and Martha serving, his sister Mary brings out a costly perfume.
JHN.12.26: In Jerusalem before the Passover, after saying a grain of wheat must die to bear fruit, Jesus tells those who would serve him to follow him.
JHN.12.27: In Jerusalem days before his death, Jesus openly admits his distress at the suffering ahead and asks aloud how he should pray.
JHN.14.9: At the Last Supper, Philip asks Jesus to show the disciples the Father, and Jesus answers with surprise after all their time together.
JHN.16.32: On the night before his crucifixion, as his disciples finally say they believe, Jesus warns them that they are about to scatter and leave him.
JHN.17.17: Praying for his disciples on the night before his death, Jesus asks the Father to set them apart as they remain in a world that hates them.
JHN.18.17: After Jesus is arrested, Peter follows him to the high priest's courtyard, where the servant girl keeping the door asks him a question.
JHN.19.26: Hanging on the cross, Jesus sees his mother standing nearby with the disciple he loved, and he entrusts them to each other.
JHN.21.25: Closing his Gospel after the risen Jesus' last conversation with Peter, John adds a final remark about everything he could not include.
ACT.1.11: As the apostles stare into the sky after Jesus is taken up out of their sight near Jerusalem, two men dressed in white suddenly appear beside them.
ACT.2.24: Preaching to a Jerusalem crowd on the day of Pentecost, Peter tells them that the Jesus they had put to death could not be held by death.
ACT.2.37: After Peter's Pentecost sermon declares that the Jesus they crucified is Lord and Christ, the crowd in Jerusalem is stung and turns to the apostles.
ACT.2.45: After about three thousand people are baptized at Pentecost, Luke describes how the first believers in Jerusalem looked after one another.
ACT.3.7: At the temple gate called Beautiful, after telling a man lame from birth that he has no silver or gold, Peter commands him in Jesus' name to walk.
ACT.4.24: Released after the council threatens them, Peter and John report back to the other believers, who respond to the news by praying together.
ACT.4.33: After praying for boldness in the face of threats, the Jerusalem believers share everything they own, and the apostles keep preaching.
ACT.6.15: Seized and brought before the Sanhedrin on false charges of blasphemy, Stephen faces the council as its members fix their eyes on him.
ACT.8.2: Stephen has just been stoned to death with Saul approving, and a great persecution is breaking out against the church in Jerusalem.
ACT.8.4: As Saul drags believers off to prison and persecution scatters the Jerusalem church across Judea and Samaria, Luke notes what they did next.
ACT.8.31: On a desert road, Philip finds an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah in his chariot and asks whether he understands it; this is the official's reply.
ACT.8.36: After Philip explains a passage of Isaiah as good news about Jesus, the Ethiopian official he is riding with spots water beside the road.
ACT.8.39: Philip has just baptized the Ethiopian official in water beside the road, and the two of them are coming back up out of it.
ACT.9.5: Thrown to the ground by a light from heaven near Damascus, where he was going to arrest followers of Jesus, Saul hears a voice ask why he persecutes him.
ACT.9.26: Having escaped a murder plot in Damascus by being lowered over the wall in a basket, the newly converted Saul reaches Jerusalem.
ACT.9.27: When the disciples in Jerusalem are too afraid of their former persecutor Saul to accept him, Barnabas steps in and speaks up for him.
ACT.9.36: Luke introduces a much-loved believer in the coastal town of Joppa, just before telling how she fell ill and died.
ACT.9.39: Summoned from nearby Lydda after the kind disciple Tabitha dies in Joppa, Peter arrives at the house where her body has been laid out.
ACT.10.4: A devout Roman centurion named Cornelius, who prays regularly and gives generously, sees an angel in a vision at Caesarea one afternoon.
ACT.11.24: When the Jerusalem church sends Barnabas to Antioch after hearing that Greeks there are turning to the Lord, he rejoices and encourages them.
ACT.11.29: When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, the believers in Antioch decide to help their fellow believers in Judea.
ACT.12.11: Led out of Herod's prison by an angel while thinking he is only seeing a vision, Peter finds himself alone in the street and realizes it was real.
ACT.12.24: Right after King Herod, who had persecuted the church, is struck down and dies, Luke turns back to the story of the gospel's spread.
ACT.13.48: In Pisidian Antioch, after Paul and Barnabas announce they will now take their message to the Gentiles, the non-Jewish listeners respond.
ACT.16.9: Blocked by the Spirit from preaching in Asia and Bithynia, Paul and his companions reach the port of Troas, where Paul has a vision at night.
ACT.16.26: Jailed in Philippi after freeing a slave girl whose fortune-telling spirit earned her owners money, Paul and Silas are in the inner cell at midnight when this happens.
ACT.16.33: After the Philippian jailer asks how to be saved and hears Paul and Silas speak about Jesus, he tends to the two men that same night.
ACT.17.30: Addressing the council of the Areopagus in Athens, a city full of idols, Paul reaches the turning point of his speech about the unknown God.
ACT.20.10: During Paul's long talk at Troas, a young man named Eutychus dozes off in a window and falls three stories, and he is picked up dead.
ACT.20.22: Saying farewell to the elders of the Ephesian church at Miletus, Paul tells them where he is headed next and how little he knows of what awaits.
ACT.20.28: Later in his farewell at Miletus, having told the Ephesian elders they will not see him again, Paul gives them a charge for the church.
ACT.21.5: After a week with the believers in Tyre on the way to Jerusalem, Paul and his traveling companions prepare to board their ship again.
ACT.23.1: Brought by the Roman commander before the Jewish council in Jerusalem after a riot, Paul looks its members in the eye and begins his defense.
ACT.24.25: Held under guard in Caesarea, Paul is called to speak about faith in Christ to the Roman governor Felix and his wife Drusilla.
ACT.26.19: Defending himself before King Agrippa in Caesarea, Paul finishes recounting how the risen Jesus met him and sent him to the Gentiles.
ACT.26.28: As Paul presses King Agrippa about believing the prophets during his defense in Caesarea, the king answers him with this remark.
ACT.26.29: Standing in chains before King Agrippa and the governor Festus, Paul answers the king's remark about being persuaded to become a Christian.
ACT.27.20: Sailing with Paul, a prisoner bound for Rome, Luke recalls days of storm with no sun or stars, until everyone on board gave up hope of rescue.
ACT.27.29: Around midnight on the fourteenth night of the storm, the sailors take soundings and find the water growing shallower as the ship drifts toward unseen land.
ACT.27.34: Just before dawn, after soldiers cut loose the lifeboat some sailors meant to flee in, Paul speaks to everyone on board, who have gone two weeks without a proper meal.
ACT.27.44: After the centurion stops a plan to kill the prisoners, the swimmers from Paul's wrecked ship head for shore, and the rest follow on planks and broken pieces.
ROM.1.8: Opening his letter to the believers in Rome, a church he had not yet visited, Paul thanks God that their faith is being talked about everywhere.
ACT.28.5: Shipwrecked on Malta, Paul is bitten by a viper while adding sticks to a fire, and the islanders watch him, expecting him to fall down dead.
ACT.28.31: In the closing words of Acts, Paul spends two years in a rented house in Rome as a prisoner, welcoming visitors and teaching about Jesus.
1CO.1.4: Before taking up the divisions troubling the church in Corinth, Paul, writing with Sosthenes, begins by thanking God for the grace they have received in Christ.
2CO.9.11: Urging the Corinthians to finish their collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, Paul looks past the gift itself to the thanks it will stir up.
GAL.2.21: Recounting how he confronted Peter at Antioch for drawing back from Gentile believers, Paul tells the Galatians why he will not return to living under the law.
GAL.3.13: Quoting the law of Moses, Paul tells the Galatian churches that Christ freed them from the law's curse by bearing that curse himself on the cross.
GAL.3.27: Telling the Galatians they are no longer under the law's supervision, Paul describes baptism into Christ as being clothed with Christ himself.
GAL.3.29: Answering teachers who said Gentile believers must be circumcised, Paul tells the Galatians that belonging to Christ already makes them Abraham's heirs.
GAL.4.14: Pleading with the Galatians, Paul recalls how they welcomed him like an angel of God when an illness, a real burden to them, first brought him among them.
GAL.5.7: Grieved that the Galatians are being drawn toward circumcision and the law, Paul reminds them how well they had been running and asks who cut in on them.
GAL.5.9: Warning the Galatians about the teachers pressing circumcision on them, Paul quotes a saying about how a little yeast spreads through the whole batch of dough.
GAL.5.17: Explaining why the Galatians must walk by the Spirit, Paul describes a constant tug-of-war inside believers between the Spirit and their sinful desires.
GAL.5.26: Right after urging the Galatians to keep in step with the Spirit, Paul warns them against the pride and envy that set believers against each other.
GAL.6.3: Between telling the Galatians to carry each other's burdens and to test their own work, Paul warns them against an inflated view of themselves.
EPH.2.14: Writing to non-Jewish believers in Ephesus, Paul says Christ has broken down the wall of hostility that once divided Jews and Gentiles.
EPH.2.22: Telling Gentile believers in Ephesus they are no longer outsiders but members of God's household, Paul pictures them being built together into a home for God.
EPH.3.13: Writing as a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, Paul asks the Ephesians not to lose heart over what he is suffering on their behalf.
EPH.4.7: After urging the Ephesians to keep the unity of one body and one Spirit, Paul adds that each believer has been given grace as Christ chose to give it.
EPH.4.14: Describing the apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers Christ gave to equip his people, Paul tells the Ephesians what that growth should lead to.
EPH.4.28: Spelling out what their new life looks like in practice, Paul tells former thieves in the Ephesian church to work honestly so they can give to people in need.
EPH.4.30: Between warnings about harmful speech and bitterness, Paul tells the Ephesians not to grieve the Holy Spirit, with whom God has sealed them as his own.
EPH.5.14: Urging the Ephesians to live as people of the light, Paul quotes what seems to be an early Christian hymn calling sleepers to wake up.
EPH.5.25: In instructions for Christian households, Paul tells husbands in Ephesus to love their wives the way Christ loved the church and gave himself for it.
EPH.6.4: After telling the children of the Ephesian church to honor their parents, Paul turns to fathers and tells them how to raise their children.
EPH.6.12: As he tells the Ephesians to put on God's armor, Paul explains that their real struggle is not with other people but with unseen spiritual powers of evil.
EPH.6.18: After describing each piece of God's armor, from the belt of truth to the sword of the Spirit, Paul tells the Ephesians to keep praying at all times.
PHP.1.8: Writing from prison to the church at Philippi, his partners in the gospel from the very start, Paul tells them how deeply he longs for them.
PHP.1.14: Writing in chains, Paul tells the Philippians that his imprisonment has made most of the believers around him bolder in speaking about Christ.
PHP.1.20: In chains, with the outcome of his case still unknown, Paul tells the Philippians he hopes to honor Christ boldly, whether he lives or dies.
PHP.1.23: Weighing his possible death while in prison, Paul tells the Philippians he is torn between going to be with Christ and staying to serve them.
PHP.2.8: Urging the Philippians to share the humble mindset of Jesus, Paul traces how Christ, though equal with God, came as a man and humbled himself.
PHP.2.12: Right after describing how God exalted the humbled Christ, Paul urges the Philippians, who obeyed him when he was with them, to keep going in his absence.
PHP.3.7: After listing his impressive credentials as a law-keeping Pharisee, Paul tells the Philippians he now counts all of it as loss for Christ's sake.
PHP.4.1: Right after reminding the Philippians that their true citizenship is in heaven, Paul calls them his joy and crown and urges them to stand firm.
PHP.4.18: Acknowledging the gifts the Philippian church sent him in prison, Paul says he now has more than enough and calls their gift an offering pleasing to God.
COL.1.24: Writing from prison to the believers in Colossae, Paul says he rejoices in what he suffers for them and for the church, which is Christ's body.
COL.2.8: Warning the Colossians about teachers with persuasive arguments, Paul tells them not to be taken captive by empty philosophy built on human tradition.
COL.2.15: Explaining what God did through Christ's cross, Paul tells the Colossians that God disarmed the hostile spiritual powers and put their defeat on public display.
COL.3.4: Having told the Colossians their life is now hidden with Christ in God, Paul looks ahead to the day Christ appears and they share in his glory.
COL.3.8: Reminding the Colossians of the ways they once lived, Paul tells them to strip off anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy talk like old clothes.
COL.3.20: In household instructions to the Colossian church, after addressing wives and husbands, Paul speaks directly to the children.
COL.4.12: Closing his letter, Paul passes on greetings from Epaphras, the Colossian from whom they first learned the gospel, who keeps praying hard for them.
COL.4.17: In the final greetings of his letter, Paul asks the Colossian church to pass on a personal charge to Archippus about the ministry he has received.
1TH.1.6: Opening their letter, Paul, Silvanus and Timothy recall how the Thessalonians received the gospel with joy from the Holy Spirit despite heavy suffering.
1TH.2.7: Insisting they came to Thessalonica without flattery, greed or demands, Paul, Silvanus and Timothy recall how they treated the new believers there.
1TH.2.17: Forced to leave Thessalonica soon after the church began, Paul and his companions tell the believers there how intensely they long to see them again.
1TH.2.20: Explaining that Satan blocked his repeated attempts to return, Paul tells the Thessalonian believers what they mean to him and his companions.
1TH.3.9: After Timothy returns from Thessalonica with good news of the church's faith and love, Paul and his companions struggle to find enough thanks for them.
1TH.4.7: Instructing the Thessalonian church on sexual conduct, Paul reminds them that God's call is to a holy life, not an impure one.
1TH.4.9: Turning to the subject of love among believers, Paul tells the Thessalonians they hardly need his instruction, since God has already taught them.
1TH.5.10: Writing to a church grieving members who had died, Paul says Christ died so that believers, whether alive or dead when he returns, will live with him.
1TH.5.19: Among the rapid-fire commands that close his letter to the Thessalonians, Paul warns them not to put out the Spirit's fire among them.
2TH.3.1: Near the end of their second letter, Paul, Silvanus and Timothy ask the Thessalonians to pray that the Lord's message spreads quickly.
1TI.1.12: Writing to Timothy, whom he had left in Ephesus to stop false teaching, Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and trusting him with ministry.
1TI.1.13: Thanking Christ for appointing him to serve, Paul tells Timothy plainly what kind of man he was before he received that mercy.
1TI.2.8: Instructing Timothy on worship in the Ephesian church, Paul asks that the men pray with lifted hands, free of anger and arguing.
1TI.4.7: Warning Timothy about teachers who forbid marriage and certain foods, Paul tells him to reject silly myths and train himself in godliness instead.
1TI.4.14: Instructing Timothy on leading the church in Ephesus, Paul urges him not to neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him with a prophetic word.
1TI.5.5: Giving Timothy guidance on how the Ephesian church should care for widows, Paul describes a widow left all alone who puts her hope in God.
1TI.6.11: Right after warning that the love of money has led some away from the faith, Paul addresses Timothy directly as a 'man of God.'
2TI.1.4: Writing from prison in what is likely his last letter, Paul tells Timothy that he remembers Timothy's tears and longs to see him again.
2TI.1.6: Imprisoned and near the end of his life, Paul urges Timothy not to be timid but to fan into flame the gift he received when Paul laid hands on him.
2TI.1.8: Writing as a prisoner, Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the message about Jesus or of Paul's chains, but to share in suffering for the gospel.
2TI.1.14: Just before naming those in Asia who deserted him, Paul tells Timothy to guard the teaching entrusted to him with the Holy Spirit's help.
2TI.2.3: Asking Timothy to pass on his teaching to faithful people, Paul calls him to endure hardship alongside him like a good soldier of Christ.
2TI.2.21: Using the picture of a large house with honored and common vessels, Paul tells Timothy how a person can be made ready for every good work.
2TI.2.23: With false teachers stirring up arguments in the church, Paul tells Timothy, as the Lord's servant, to refuse the foolish debates that only breed fights.
2TI.3.15: Writing to Timothy, whose mother and grandmother shared their faith with him, Paul reminds him of the Scriptures he has known from infancy.
2TI.4.6: Writing from prison and expecting execution, Paul tells Timothy why he must carry on the work: Paul's own time is almost over.
2TI.4.11: Deserted by Demas and missing his other coworkers, Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark, whom he had once refused to take along on a mission journey.
TIT.3.3: Telling Titus how believers in Crete should treat outsiders, Paul admits that he and they once lived the same way, before God's kindness appeared.
TIT.3.9: Closing his instructions to Titus for the churches in Crete, Paul tells him to steer clear of pointless quarrels over genealogies and the law.
PHM.1.9: An old man now and a prisoner, Paul writes to Philemon about his slave Onesimus, choosing to make his request out of love rather than as an order.
PHM.1.20: After offering to repay anything Onesimus owes, Paul asks Philemon to refresh his heart by welcoming Onesimus back as a brother.
HEB.10.25: Warning believers under pressure not to drift away from Christ, the writer of Hebrews turns from their private hope to their life together as a church.
JAS.3.5: Warning would-be teachers about the power of words, James compares the tongue to a horse's bit, a ship's rudder and a small spark.
1PE.1.13: After describing a salvation the prophets longed to understand, Peter urges scattered believers to ready their minds and fix their hope on Christ's return.
1PE.1.23: Urging scattered believers to love one another deeply, Peter reminds them they have been born again through God's living and lasting word.
1PE.2.16: Telling believers scattered across Asia Minor to respect human authorities, Peter reminds them they are free, but free as God's servants.
1PE.2.19: Addressing household servants with harsh masters, Peter says that bearing unjust suffering out of awareness of God is commendable.
2CO.5.18: Defending his ministry to the Corinthians, Paul explains that the love of Christ compels him and his coworkers, and traces their whole message back to God.
1PE.3.13: After quoting a psalm about God's eyes on the righteous, Peter asks believers facing hostility who can really harm those eager to do good.
1PE.4.7: Writing to believers mocked for no longer joining their old way of life, Peter tells them the end is near and calls them to clear, prayerful minds.
1PE.4.9: Among instructions for a church under pressure, right after urging deep love, Peter tells believers to open their homes to each other without grumbling.
1PE.4.11: Having told believers to use their gifts to serve one another, Peter explains how both speakers and servers should do it, so that God gets the glory.
1PE.4.14: Writing to believers facing a fiery trial, Peter tells those insulted for bearing Christ's name that God's Spirit rests on them.
2PE.1.16: Expecting his death soon, Peter insists his message about Jesus came from eyewitnesses, not clever myths, before recalling the voice he heard on the mountain.
2PE.3.15: Answering scoffers who ask why Christ has not returned, Peter says the Lord's patience means salvation, adding that Paul wrote the same.
2PE.3.17: Closing his second letter, Peter warns believers who know the truth not to be swept away by lawless people who twist Scripture.
1JN.4.20: Having written that love comes from God, John confronts anyone who claims to love God while hating a fellow believer.
2JN.1.5: Writing to 'the chosen lady' and her children, the elder asks them to keep the command they have had from the beginning: love one another.
2JN.1.8: After warning 'the chosen lady' about deceivers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh, the elder urges her and her children to guard what has been worked for.
2JN.1.12: Closing his short letter to 'the chosen lady' and her children, the elder says he would rather visit in person than write more with paper and ink.
3JN.1.5: Writing to his friend Gaius, the elder praises him for faithfully welcoming traveling believers, even ones he did not know.
REV.2.4: In his message to the church in Ephesus, praised for hard work and for exposing false apostles, the risen Jesus names what they have lost.
GEN.3.9: After Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit and hide among the trees at the sound of God walking in the garden, God calls out to Adam.
GEN.3.21: After pronouncing the painful consequences of their disobedience, God himself provides for Adam and Eve, who had covered themselves with fig leaves.
GEN.32.24: Afraid to face Esau, the brother he had cheated years before, Jacob sends his family and everything he owns across the Jabbok and stays behind.
GEN.42.36: Back from buying grain in Egypt, Jacob's sons report that Simeon is held there and Benjamin must go next, and their father, still mourning Joseph, cries out.
GEN.45.24: Having revealed himself to the brothers who once sold him into slavery, Joseph loads them with gifts and sends them home to bring their father Jacob to Egypt.
GEN.49.18: In the middle of blessing each of his twelve sons from his deathbed, the aged Jacob pauses to speak directly to God.
EXO.2.24: Years pass while Moses lives as a foreigner in Midian, and back in Egypt, after the old king dies, the enslaved Israelites keep crying out under their burdens.
EXO.4.13: Having run out of excuses, and even after God's promise to give him the words, Moses makes a final, blunter plea at the burning bush.
GEN.2.2: Closing the account of creation, after six days of forming the heavens, the earth and all that lives in them, Genesis describes the seventh day.
EXO.32.30: The day after the golden calf and the bloodshed that followed in the camp, Moses confronts the people and tells them what he plans to do.
EXO.33.15: Still pleading for Israel at the tent of meeting, Moses answers God's promise of his Presence by making clear how much depends on it.
LEV.6.13: Giving Moses the rules Aaron and his sons must follow for the burnt offering, God stresses one duty about the altar more than once.
LEV.10.3: Moments after fire from the Lord kills Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu for offering unauthorized fire, Moses speaks to their grieving father.
LEV.19.10: Right after telling Israel not to reap to the very edges of their fields, God turns through Moses to the grape harvest.
LEV.23.3: Opening a list of Israel's appointed feasts and sacred assemblies, God tells Moses what comes first, before any yearly festival.
LEV.25.23: In laws for the Jubilee, when every fiftieth year family land returned to its original owners, God tells Israel who truly owns the land.
LEV.26.9: In a passage of promises for a faithful Israel, God follows a picture of five soldiers routing a hundred with a promise about the nation's growth.
NUM.11.17: God responds to Moses' desperate prayer by telling him to gather seventy of Israel's elders at the Tent of Meeting.
EXO.14.31: Safe on the far side of the sea they had crossed on dry ground, the Israelites see the bodies of Pharaoh's soldiers washed up on the shore.
NUM.21.8: After Moses prays for the people, who have been dying from venomous snake bites in the wilderness, God gives him an unusual instruction.
NUM.23.20: Standing beside Balak and the princes of Moab on the heights of Pisgah, Balaam tells the king of Moab why he cannot give him the curse on Israel he wants.
NUM.24.5: Looking out over Israel camped tribe by tribe in the wilderness, Balaam feels the Spirit of God come on him and begins his third oracle.
DEU.1.21: Retelling Israel's journey from Mount Horeb, Moses recalls what he said when the people first reached Kadesh-barnea at the edge of the Amorite hill country.
DEU.4.7: Urging Israel to keep God's laws carefully in the land ahead, Moses says the surrounding nations will notice, and asks what makes this people truly great.
DEU.4.39: Recalling how God spoke from the fire and brought them out of Egypt with great power, Moses draws the conclusion he wants Israel to carry into the new land.
DEU.6.6: Right after calling Israel to love God with all their heart, soul and strength, Moses tells the people where these commands belong.
DEU.7.7: Having called Israel God's treasured possession among all peoples, Moses heads off any pride the nation might take in being chosen.
DEU.30.6: Looking far ahead to a time when Israel will be scattered among the nations and then brought home, Moses describes what God will do inside his people.
DEU.30.11: Having set before Israel the blessings and curses of the covenant made in Moab, Moses turns to whether the people can actually keep God's commands.
DEU.33.28: Finishing his blessings on the tribes one by one, the aged Moses turns to the whole nation and the God who shelters it.
JOS.6.27: After the walls of Jericho fall and Rahab's family is spared, the account of Israel's first victory in Canaan closes with a word about Joshua.
JOS.10.14: Defending Gibeon against five Amorite kings, Joshua asks for the sun and moon to stand still, and the narrator pauses over what happened that day.
JOS.21.43: Centuries after God promised a homeland to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the tribes of Israel are now living in towns and fields spread across Canaan.
JOS.23.8: Warning Israel's leaders not to call on or bow to the gods of the nations still living around them, Joshua sets out what they should do instead.
JOS.24.14: Having reminded Israel that they live in cities they did not build and eat from vineyards they did not plant, Joshua calls for a response.
JDG.6.40: Worried he is pressing his luck, Gideon has asked God not to be angry with one more fleece test before he leads Israel against Midian.
JDG.7.2: Camped by the spring of Harod with the Midianite army in the valley to the north, Gideon has gathered a large force, and God speaks to him about its size.
JDG.8.23: After Gideon's small army routs Midian and he executes its kings Zebah and Zalmunna, the grateful Israelites ask him to found a ruling dynasty.
JDG.10.10: For eighteen years the Ammonites and Philistines have oppressed the Israelites east of the Jordan, and as the Ammonites cross the river to attack, the people finally cry out.
JDG.13.18: Manoah, who does not yet realize his visitor is the angel of the Lord, asks for his name so he can honor him when his promise of a son comes true.
JDG.15.18: Having killed a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone at Lehi, Samson is suddenly desperate with thirst.
RUT.1.14: On the road back to Judah, Naomi urges her two widowed daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' homes in Moab, since she has no more sons to give them.
RUT.2.4: While Ruth is gleaning in a field that happens to belong to Boaz, a relative of Naomi's late husband, the owner himself arrives from town.
RUT.3.1: As the harvest season in Bethlehem draws to a close, Naomi turns her thoughts to the future of Ruth, the widowed Moabite daughter-in-law who has cared for her.
RUT.3.10: Startled awake at midnight to find Ruth lying at his feet and asking him to spread his garment over her, Boaz responds warmly.
RUT.3.18: Ruth comes home at dawn from the threshing floor with six measures of barley from Boaz and tells Naomi everything, and Naomi, who knows the man, answers her.
RUT.4.16: Naomi, who once came back to Bethlehem saying the Lord had brought her home empty, is handed the newborn son that Ruth has borne to Boaz.
1SA.2.6: Having left her young son Samuel to serve at the house of the Lord in Shiloh, Hannah prays a song about how God reverses people's fortunes.
1SA.7.3: Twenty years after the ark came back from the Philistines to Kiriath-jearim, as Israel mourns and seeks God, Samuel speaks to the whole nation.
1SA.12.21: Telling the terrified Israelites not to fear even though asking for a king was wrong, Samuel adds a warning about what they might chase instead.
1SA.20.3: Having fled to Jonathan from Naioth in Ramah, David hears his friend insist that King Saul would never plot against him without telling his own son.
1SA.20.41: Hiding in the field where he and Jonathan agreed to meet, David waits by a stone until Jonathan's servant boy, who knows nothing of their plan, is sent back to the city.
1SA.24.10: Having spared King Saul in a cave at En-gedi and cut off only the corner of his robe, David steps out and calls after the king who has been hunting him.
1SA.25.35: Talked out of slaughtering Nabal's household by Nabal's wise wife Abigail, David now turns to the gifts of food she has brought him.
JOS.7.7: After Israel's small force is routed at the little town of Ai, Joshua tears his clothes and lies facedown before the ark until evening.
2SA.1.19: Having heard that Saul and his son Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines, David composes a lament for them called the Song of the Bow.
2SA.7.20: Still stunned that God's promise reaches beyond his own lifetime to the future of his house, King David continues his prayer of thanks.
2SA.12.16: When the infant son Bathsheba bore him falls seriously ill, as the prophet Nathan had warned, King David turns to God on the child's behalf.
2SA.13.37: After Absalom has his half-brother Amnon killed for assaulting his sister Tamar, King David's household weeps and Absalom runs for his life.
2SA.15.21: Fleeing Jerusalem as his son Absalom seizes power, King David urges Ittai of Gath, a foreigner who had only just joined him, to go back.
2SA.15.26: Crossing the Kidron Valley as he flees, David sends the priest Zadok back to Jerusalem with the ark and speaks about whether he will ever see the city again.
2SA.24.10: Joab returns after nearly ten months of counting Israel's fighting men for the census he had urged King David not to take.
1KI.3.5: Early in his reign, Solomon travels to the great high place at Gibeon and offers a thousand burnt offerings on its altar.
1KI.8.18: Speaking to the assembled nation at the dedication of the new temple, King Solomon recalls the plan that had long been in his father David's heart.
1KI.8.58: Having asked that God stay with Israel as he stayed with their ancestors, King Solomon goes on in his blessing to ask for something within the people themselves.
1KI.17.6: After announcing a drought to King Ahab, Elijah obeys God's command to hide by the Brook of Cherith east of the Jordan.
1KI.17.24: When the son of the widow who has been sheltering Elijah in Zarephath dies and is brought back to life, Elijah carries the boy down to his mother.
1KI.18.37: On Mount Carmel, after Baal's prophets have shouted all day with no answer, Elijah drenches his altar and sacrifice with water and then prays.
1KI.18.44: At the end of a long drought, Elijah crouches on the summit of Carmel with his face between his knees and keeps sending his servant to look toward the sea.
1KI.19.21: When the prophet Elijah throws his cloak over Elisha as he plows with the twelfth pair of oxen, Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye first.
2KI.2.9: Knowing God will take Elijah away that day, Elisha refuses to leave his side, and the two cross the Jordan on dry ground after Elijah strikes the water.
2KI.2.12: Walking and talking with Elijah beyond the Jordan, Elisha sees a chariot and horses of fire suddenly separate them as his master is taken up.
2KI.4.2: A widow whose husband was one of the prophets' disciples begs Elisha for help, because a creditor is coming to take her two sons as slaves.
2KI.5.13: Insulted that Elisha only sent a messenger telling him to wash in the Jordan, the Aramean commander Naaman storms off in a rage.
2KI.5.15: Healed of leprosy after dipping seven times in the Jordan, Naaman returns with his whole entourage to the house of the prophet Elisha.
2KI.6.15: Furious that Elisha keeps warning Israel's king about his plans, the king of Aram sends horses, chariots and a great army by night to seize the prophet at Dothan.
2KI.6.23: Holding a captured band of Aramean raiders inside Samaria, Israel's king follows Elisha's surprising advice to treat his enemies as guests.
1CH.4.9: In Hebrew the name Jabez echoes the word for pain, and this otherwise unknown man from Judah's clans is given only two verses in the whole Bible.
1CH.13.8: Bringing the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim on a new cart, David gathers Israelites from all over the land to accompany it.
1CH.22.12: Having told Solomon that God chose him, a man of peace, to build the temple, David turns from the building project to the kind of king his son must be.
1CH.23.25: As the aging King David organizes the Levites for service in the future temple, he explains why their old duty of carrying the tabernacle is ending.
1CH.29.17: Having given his own treasure of gold and silver toward the temple Solomon will build, the aged King David watches the leaders of Israel follow his lead.
2CH.7.15: God answers the long prayer Solomon offered at the temple's dedication, taking up the king's own request that God watch over this house day and night.
2CH.13.18: When King Abijah of Judah is ambushed front and rear by the larger army of Jeroboam of Israel, the men of Judah cry out and the priests blow the trumpets.
2CH.14.6: Early in his reign, King Asa of Judah tears down foreign altars and idols and commands the people to seek the Lord, and the kingdom enjoys a time of quiet.
2CH.15.17: After King Asa deposes the queen mother Maacah for making an Asherah pole and burns it in the Kidron Valley, the chronicler sums up the king's reforms.
2CH.20.9: With armies from Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir marching on Judah, Jehoshaphat stands in the temple courtyard and reminds God of what Israel said when building it.
2CH.30.20: At King Hezekiah's great Passover in Jerusalem, many worshippers from the northern tribes eat the meal without being ritually purified, and the king prays for them.
2CH.32.26: After God rescues Jerusalem from Sennacherib of Assyria and heals Hezekiah of a deadly illness, the king grows proud instead of grateful.
2CH.34.3: Josiah became king of Judah at only eight years old, and the chronicler traces how his faith and his reforms grew as he came of age.
EZR.1.6: When Persia's King Cyrus lets the exiles return to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, the families of Judah and Benjamin prepare for the long journey home.
GEN.35.3: Told by God to go back to Bethel, where God had appeared to him as he fled from Esau, Jacob has his household get rid of their foreign gods.
NEH.4.20: With enemies threatening to attack, Nehemiah has half his men stand guard while the builders work with swords at their sides, spread thin along Jerusalem's wall.
EZR.6.14: Once King Darius of Persia confirms Cyrus's decree and orders the local governor not to interfere, the Jewish elders press on with rebuilding the temple.
EZR.10.1: Devastated to learn how many of the returned exiles have broken faith with God, Ezra has prayed a long confession on the people's behalf at the temple.
NEH.1.10: Grieving over news that Jerusalem's walls lie broken, Nehemiah confesses Israel's sins in prayer and reminds God of his promise to gather the scattered exiles.
NEH.2.8: Given a chance to speak to King Artaxerxes, Nehemiah asks to be sent to rebuild Jerusalem and then requests letters to make the journey and the work possible.
NEH.2.17: Nearly a century and a half after Babylon burned Jerusalem, Nehemiah, newly arrived from the Persian court, speaks to the priests, nobles and officials of Judah.
NEH.6.11: A man named Shemaiah warns Nehemiah that assassins are coming at night and urges him to hide inside the temple with the doors shut.
NEH.9.6: After the returned exiles spend hours hearing the Law read and confessing their sins, the Levites lead them in a long prayer that begins with creation.
NEH.9.20: After recalling the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, the Levites' prayer turns to God's other gifts to Israel in the desert.
NEH.9.28: Recalling the generations after Joshua, when Israel lived in Canaan without a king, the Levites turn to the era of the judges.
NEH.9.32: Having traced Israel's long story of rebellion and rescue, the Levites leading the returned exiles' confession turn from the past to their own hard present.
EXO.33.11: Describing the tent Moses pitched outside the camp, the narrator tells how God met him there while the people watched from their own tent doors.
EST.3.2: After King Xerxes promotes Haman above all his nobles, the officials at the palace gate face a royal order to honor him, and Mordecai the Jew takes a stand.
EST.4.3: As copies of Haman's decree reach the provinces of the Persian empire, Jewish communities far beyond the capital learn they have been marked for destruction.
EST.4.11: Handed a copy of Haman's decree through the servant Hathach, Queen Esther hears Mordecai's plea that she go to the king for her people.
EST.5.1: After three days in which she and the Jews of Susa have fasted for her, Queen Esther dresses in her royal robes and goes to face the king.
EST.5.3: Having just spared Esther's life by holding out his gold scepter, King Xerxes turns to her with a generous question.
DEU.10.21: After urging Israel to love the foreigner because they were once foreigners in Egypt, Moses sums up who their God is to them.
HEB.3.6: After honoring Moses as a faithful servant in God's household, the writer of Hebrews turns to Christ, the Son over it, and to his readers' place within it.
JOB.7.7: In the middle of his first reply to Eliphaz, Job stops speaking to his friends and pleads with God himself about how short his life feels.
JOB.9.8: Replying to Bildad, Job admits no one can win an argument with God, then describes a God who shakes the earth and seals off the stars.
JOB.10.11: After comparing his conception to milk curdling into cheese, Job keeps tracing, in words addressed to God, how his body took shape before birth.
JOB.12.22: Answering Zophar, Job shows he knows God's greatness as well as his friends do, describing how God overturns kings, elders and whole nations.
JOB.14.15: After wishing God would hide him in the grave until his anger passes, Job lets himself imagine the day that waiting would end.
JOB.19.27: Having wished his words could be carved in rock forever, Job carries his confession of hope one step further, and the longing behind it overwhelms him.
JOB.23.11: Eliphaz has just urged Job to repent and return to the Almighty, and Job answers that his record is not what his friend assumes.
JOB.26.14: After describing God's command of the sky, the sea and even the realm of the dead, Job brings this part of his reply to Bildad to a close in awe.
JOB.29.16: In his closing defense, Job remembers how elders stood up and princes fell silent when he took his seat at the city gate.
JOB.30.16: Having described the jeering crowds and terrors that now surround him, Job turns inward to the misery that has taken hold of him.
JOB.30.25: Feeling abandoned by God and ignored by everyone as he cries for help, Job points to the compassion he once showed people in trouble.
JOB.9.33: Still answering Bildad, Job says that even scrubbing himself with snow and lye could not make him clean enough to stand trial before God.
JOB.38.41: Answering Job out of the storm, God points him to the lions crouched in their dens and to other wild creatures that no human feeds.
JOB.40.4: Challenged by God to answer after the first speech from the storm, Job, who had long demanded a hearing with God, finally responds.
JOB.42.9: Told by God that they had spoken wrongly about him, Job's three friends bring the sacrifices God required and depend on Job to pray for them.
JOB.42.11: Once his ordeal is over, Job welcomes into his home the relatives and old friends he had earlier complained had turned away from him.
PRO.3.23: Urging his son to hold on to sound judgment and discernment, Solomon describes what such wisdom will mean for his daily walk.
PRO.4.26: Moving from the heart to the mouth, eyes and feet, Solomon walks his son through how to keep his life pointed in one direction.
PRO.10.7: Early in the first long collection of his two-line sayings, Solomon looks past a person's lifetime to how they will be remembered.
PRO.12.15: Among his sayings on work, speech and good sense, Solomon turns to how a person decides whether his own plans are sound.
PRO.14.32: Following a saying about kindness to the poor, Solomon looks to the end of life and what each kind of person has to lean on there.
PRO.15.29: In a cluster of sayings about what pleases or grieves the Lord, Solomon turns to the question of who is near to God and who is far away.
PRO.16.31: Coming after sketches of gossips and violent schemers, this saying of Solomon's turns to the dignity of someone who has grown old on a good path.
PRO.17.6: Looking at three generations of one family, Solomon names what the old and the young each take pride in.
PRO.19.8: Amid sayings about fair-weather friends and false witnesses, Solomon points to what a person gains by seeking wisdom.
PRO.19.14: Just after a saying about a quarrelsome wife, Solomon contrasts what parents can pass down with a blessing only the Lord can give.
PRO.20.7: Following a question about who can find a truly trustworthy person, this proverb looks at how one faithful life affects a family.
PRO.20.27: Among sayings about kings, vows and honest weights, Solomon turns from what people show outwardly to what lies deep inside them.
PRO.21.1: Drawing on the way a farmer channels irrigation water, Solomon speaks about who truly holds power over the rulers of the earth.
PRO.23.26: After telling his son how much his parents long to see him grow wise, Solomon makes a direct, personal request of him.
ECC.1.7: Having watched the sun hurry back to where it rises and the wind circle round, the Preacher looks next at the streams that feed the sea.
ECC.3.10: Right after his well-known poem about a time for everything, the Preacher asks what workers gain from their toil and shares what he has observed.
ECC.3.20: Troubled by injustice even in courts of law, the Preacher compares the death of human beings with the death of animals.
ECC.4.8: Having just said one quiet handful beats two handfuls of toil, the Preacher turns to a lonely figure he has watched under the sun.
ECC.5.1: After reflecting on lonely toil and on crowds who cheer a new young king and then forget him, the Preacher turns to how people carry themselves in worship.
ECC.5.15: After describing a man who loses his fortune in a bad venture and has nothing left for his son, the Preacher reflects on how everyone leaves this world.
ECC.6.7: Weighing long, prosperous lives that are never actually enjoyed, the Preacher considers why human effort never seems to be enough.
ECC.7.5: Continuing to compare the house of mourning with the house of pleasure, the Preacher weighs two very different things a person might listen to.
ECC.7.19: Having warned against extremes of both righteousness and wickedness, the Preacher sets the worth of wisdom against the power of a city's rulers.
ECC.8.12: Troubled that justice is slow and the wicked often live long lives, the Preacher still holds to what he knows about those who fear God.
ECC.11.2: Following his picture of bread cast on the water, the Preacher gives a second piece of advice about sharing in an uncertain world.
ECC.11.9: Having urged readers to rejoice in every year they are given, the Preacher now addresses the young and the choices of their early years.
SNG.2.1: Trading words of admiration with her beloved, the young woman describes herself with images of flowers from Israel's plains and valleys.
SNG.2.2: Hearing the young woman compare herself to wildflowers of the valley, the man who loves her takes up her own image and turns it into praise.
SNG.2.8: After urging the young women of Jerusalem not to stir up love too soon, the bride catches the first sound of her beloved on his way to her.
SNG.3.4: Having gone out through the city streets at night and questioned the watchmen, the young woman describes the end of her anxious search.
SNG.5.8: After her beloved slips away from her door and the city watchmen beat her in the streets, the young woman calls on Jerusalem's women for help.
SNG.5.10: When the women of Jerusalem ask what makes her beloved so special, the young woman begins a detailed portrait of him.
SNG.7.6: Having described his bride's beauty from her feet to her hair, the young man sums up his delight in her.
SNG.7.11: Declaring that she belongs to her beloved and that he desires her, the young woman makes an invitation of her own.
PSA.7.10: In a psalm sung about the words of Cush the Benjamite, David asks God, who searches hearts, to judge between him and his accusers.
PSA.12.5: After lamenting that the faithful have vanished and boasting liars seem unstoppable, David's psalm records the Lord's own reply.
PSA.20.4: Opening with a prayer that the Lord answer in the day of trouble, David's psalm asks God to remember the king's offerings and send help from Zion.
PSA.25.15: Midway through an alphabet-shaped prayer for guidance, David pictures himself caught like an animal in a hunter's trap.
PSA.31.10: Having just thanked God for setting his feet in an open place, David swings back into lament and lays his condition before the Lord.
PSA.33.5: Calling worshipers to praise God with the harp and a new song, the psalm's writer gives reasons rooted in God's own character.
PSA.33.12: Calling the whole earth to stand in awe of the God whose word created everything, the psalm's writer considers what it means to belong to him.
PSA.38.6: With festering wounds he blames on his own folly, David describes to God how low his suffering has brought him.
PSA.38.10: Before describing how friends and relatives keep their distance from his sickness, David tells the Lord what the illness is doing inside him.
PSA.41.12: Ill and betrayed even by a close friend who once ate at his table, David rests in God's support near the close of this psalm.
PSA.44.17: In a communal lament by the sons of Korah, Israel describes being mocked by its neighbors after a defeat it cannot explain.
PSA.46.4: Right after picturing mountains crashing into roaring seas, the sons of Korah turn to a calm scene inside the city where God lives.
PSA.50.14: Pointing out that every creature on a thousand hills already belongs to him, God tells his people in Asaph's psalm what offering he truly wants.
PSA.51.13: Having begged for a clean heart and restored joy, David looks beyond his own forgiveness to others who have wandered from God.
PSA.51.14: Confronted by Nathan over Bathsheba and the killing of her husband Uriah, David names the blood on his hands as he pleads with God.
PSA.46.9: Inviting everyone to come and look at the Lord's works on the earth, the sons of Korah describe what they see on the world's battlefields.
PSA.63.5: Though surrounded by a dry and waterless land, David reaches for the image of a rich banquet to describe the state of his soul.
PSA.65.2: Opening a song of praise for worship in Zion, David addresses God in words that reach beyond Israel to all humanity.
PSA.66.10: After calling every nation to bless the God who keeps Israel's feet from slipping, the psalm's writer speaks directly to God about Israel's past.
PSA.68.35: Ending a triumphant psalm that calls every kingdom on earth to sing to God, David closes with praise for the God of Israel.
PSA.69.32: Having promised praise that pleases God more than any sacrifice of an ox, David turns to the humble people who will witness it.
PSA.71.16: Surrounded by accusers who want to see him harmed, the aging writer of this psalm resolves how he will face whatever lies ahead.
PSA.71.23: Taking up the harp and lyre as his psalm draws to a close, the writer thanks the Holy One of Israel for his faithfulness.
PSA.73.14: Looking back on the season when his faith almost slipped, Asaph recalls the complaint he nursed before he went into God's sanctuary.
PSA.77.20: Having begun this psalm unable to sleep and doubting God's love, Asaph ends by recalling the leaders God gave his people during the Exodus.
PSA.78.39: Describing how the Israelites in the desert praised God with their lips while their hearts stayed disloyal, Asaph tells how God regarded them.
PSA.81.10: In Asaph's festival psalm, God reminds Israel of the day he freed them from slavery and warns them against foreign gods.
PSA.82.3: Picturing God presiding over a heavenly court, Asaph records his rebuke of those who judge unfairly and his charge to them.
PSA.85.3: Before voicing any request, the sons of Korah open their psalm by thanking God for a past homecoming, when he brought Jacob's descendants back from captivity.
PSA.88.11: Friendless and feeling swept under by God's waves, Heman uses a string of pointed questions to plead for his life.
PSA.92.5: Praising God morning and night with harp and lyre, the psalm's writer marvels at what lies behind all that God has made.
PSA.94.3: Calling on God as the judge of the whole earth to act, the psalm's writer can no longer bear watching the arrogant celebrate.
PSA.102.11: In the prayer of someone crushed by trouble and mocked all day by enemies, the writer compares his fading life to things in nature.
PSA.106.6: Before retelling Israel's long history of rebellion, the psalm's writer includes his own generation in the confession.
PSA.106.45: At the end of a long list of Israel's failures, from Egypt to captivity among the nations, the psalm's writer describes God's response to their cries.
PSA.109.22: After calling down judgment on the accusers who repaid his love with hatred, David turns to plead for God's kindness toward himself.
PSA.116.5: Between telling what happened and what it meant, the writer of this song of thanks pauses to describe the God who heard his cry.
PSA.116.9: With the ropes of death no longer around him, the psalm's writer makes a resolution about how he will spend the life he has been given back.
PSA.119.29: In the stanza of Psalm 119 that begins with his soul clinging to the dust, the writer sets two ways of living side by side.
PSA.119.52: Mocked by arrogant people for his loyalty to God's law, the writer of Psalm 119 reaches back past his own troubles to much older memories.
PSA.119.59: In a stanza that begins by calling the Lord his portion, the Psalm 119 writer recalls a moment of honest self-examination.
PSA.119.84: Feeling like a wineskin shriveled in the smoke, the writer of Psalm 119 turns from his own weariness to the arrogant men who are hunting him.
PSA.124.7: Imagining how enemies could have swallowed Israel alive had the Lord not been on their side, David blesses God for not handing his people over as prey.
PSA.135.4: Calling the servants who stand in the temple courts to sing praise, the psalm's writer grounds that praise in God's choice of his people.
PSA.140.13: David ends this plea for rescue from slanderers and violent men on a note of settled confidence about the future of the upright.
PSA.141.8: Asking God to guard his mouth and keep him from the company of evildoers, David turns his attention from his enemies' traps to the Lord himself.
PSA.143.9: With his spirit failing and enemies pressing him, David stops recalling God's past deeds and asks plainly for rescue and shelter.
PSA.144.4: In a psalm that opens by praising God for training his hands for battle, David stops to ask why the Lord pays any attention to people at all.
PSA.145.15: Having praised the Lord as a King whose rule lasts through all generations, David turns to the ordinary way this King cares for his realm day by day.
PSA.147.14: Addressing Jerusalem, whose scattered exiles God has gathered home, the psalm's writer describes the security and plenty God gives the city.
ISA.26.8: Voicing a faithful people who have watched God humble a proud city, Isaiah describes their patient waiting and the deepest desire of their hearts.
ISA.26.9: Where the song before this line spoke for a whole waiting people, Isaiah now shifts to the first person and to the hours when he prays.
ISA.29.19: After condemning people who hide their schemes from God, Isaiah looks ahead to a day when the deaf will hear and the blind will see.
ISA.33.22: Looking ahead to a Jerusalem free of foreign invaders, Isaiah pictures the city as a quiet, secure home with God himself as its protector.
ISA.45.19: Setting God, the maker of heaven and earth, against the idols of the nations, Isaiah relays how God describes the way he has spoken to Israel.
ISA.53.1: Near the start of Isaiah's song about God's suffering servant, the prophet wonders aloud who could believe what he is about to describe.
ISA.53.11: Having described the servant's silent suffering and unjust death, Isaiah now gives God's own verdict on what that suffering will achieve.
ISA.55.2: Like a market vendor calling to passersby, God speaks through Isaiah to people wearing themselves out on things that leave them empty.
ISA.56.5: Addressing eunuchs who felt shut out of God's people because they could have no children, Isaiah brings a promise for all who hold to God's covenant.
ISA.58.6: When people complain that God ignores their fasting, God answers through Isaiah by describing the kind of fast he actually wants.
ISA.58.7: Continuing God's reply to people who fasted while mistreating their workers, Isaiah moves from breaking chains to everyday acts of care close to home.
ISA.60.18: Speaking to a Zion that had long been forsaken and despised, Isaiah promises that God will one day make the city a place of lasting safety.
ISA.63.17: Speaking for a people whose sanctuary has been trampled by enemies, Isaiah dares to ask God why he has let them wander from his ways.
JER.1.6: Called in the thirteenth year of King Josiah's reign, Jeremiah hears that God set him apart before he was born and gives his first reply.
JER.1.9: After calming Jeremiah's fear of speaking, God gives the young prophet a physical sign to mark the start of his work.
JER.2.2: In one of his earliest messages, Jeremiah is sent to the streets of Jerusalem to remind the city of how its relationship with God began.
JER.4.19: As he hears warnings of an army closing in on Judah's cities, Jeremiah cannot contain the physical anguish the coming disaster causes him.
GEN.8.1: After floodwaters had covered the earth for many days and every living thing outside the ark had perished, the story turns back to Noah and those with him.
JER.9.23: Following a grim lament over death climbing through Judah's windows, Jeremiah records God naming three things people are tempted to boast about.
JER.10.6: After mocking idols that must be carried because they cannot walk, Jeremiah bursts into praise of the living God.
JER.10.19: Warning Judah to pack up before the coming siege, Jeremiah voices the nation's grief as though its wound were his own.
JER.10.24: As reports of an army from the north reach Judah, Jeremiah turns to prayer on his people's behalf, pleading about the kind of correction they will face.
ROM.11.29: Discussing Israel's future with Gentile believers in Rome, Paul insists that God's commitment made to Israel's ancestors still stands.
JER.14.22: Ending a prayer of confession for Judah during a punishing drought, Jeremiah compares the nation's idols with the God who controls the weather.
JER.15.10: Burdened by delivering judgment on his own nation, Jeremiah voices a bitter complaint about how isolated and hated his calling has made him.
JER.15.20: Answering Jeremiah's bitter complaint that God has failed him like a mirage, God calls him to return and renews the promise he made when first calling him.
JER.17.10: Once the question is raised of who can truly know the human heart, God himself answers it through Jeremiah.
JER.20.13: Surrounded by whispers and former friends waiting for him to fall, Jeremiah commits his case to God and breaks into a brief song of praise.
JER.20.18: Close on the heels of a burst of praise, Jeremiah sinks into one of his darkest laments, cursing the day he was born.
1CH.29.18: Praying aloud before the whole assembly in Jerusalem, David turns from the gifts laid out for the temple to the hearts of the people who gave them.
JER.23.24: In Jeremiah's long rebuke of Judah's false prophets, God asks whether they think he is only near at hand and not far away as well.
JER.23.29: Tired of prophets who pass off their own dreams as his message, God compares their words to straw and sets his own word against them.
JER.29.5: Sending word from Jerusalem to the families already deported to Babylon, Jeremiah opens his letter with practical instructions for a long stay.
JER.31.9: Picturing the blind, the lame and women in labor among a vast crowd returning from the north, Jeremiah describes how God will bring them home.
JER.31.10: Turning from Israel to the wider world, God tells distant nations and far-off coastlands to hear what he plans for his scattered people.
NEH.8.12: On the first day of the seventh month, after Ezra has read the Law aloud from daybreak to noon, the Levites finally quiet the crowd in Jerusalem.
JER.31.15: Amid promises of a joyful homecoming, Jeremiah suddenly voices inconsolable grief over Israel's lost children, a line Matthew later quotes about Jesus' infancy.
JER.31.17: Still speaking to Rachel, the grieving mother of the nation, God adds a second assurance to his call for her tears to stop.
JER.31.18: Moving from Rachel's grief to her wayward descendants, God says he has overheard Ephraim, the northern kingdom, groaning under its discipline.
JER.31.19: In the words God overhears, Ephraim moves past its plea for restoration to describe the shame that came with turning back.
1CO.13.2: Writing to a Corinthian church that prized knowledge and spectacular gifts, Paul keeps building his case that love outweighs them all.
JER.32.40: With Babylon's army surrounding Jerusalem, God tells Jeremiah that the city now facing sword and famine will one day be home to a restored people.
JER.32.41: While Jeremiah is held in the courtyard of the guard during the siege, God goes on telling him how he feels about the people he will one day bring home.
JER.36.3: In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, God tells Jeremiah to write all his messages on a scroll, hoping that Judah will finally listen.
JER.42.3: After Jerusalem's fall, army commanders and a small band of survivors come to Jeremiah and ask him to pray on their behalf.
LAM.1.20: Speaking as Jerusalem itself, the writer of Lamentations pictures the ruined city crying out to God with no one left to comfort her.
LAM.3.19: At the bleakest point of his third lament, the writer of Lamentations dwells on the bitter taste of all he has suffered.
LAM.3.39: Just after insisting that God takes no pleasure in injustice, the writer of Lamentations turns the spotlight back onto his own people and their sins.
LAM.3.41: Moving from self-examination toward prayer, the writer of Lamentations calls the whole community to join in a gesture of worship toward heaven.
REV.2.3: Speaking through John to the believers in Ephesus, the risen Jesus, who walks among the seven golden lampstands, begins by telling them what he has noticed.
LAM.3.54: Recounting how enemies hunted him like a bird and threw stones down on him, the writer of Lamentations describes the moment he gave himself up for lost.
LAM.3.56: Still recalling his ordeal in the flooded pit, the writer of Lamentations quotes the short, desperate plea he sent up to God.
LAM.5.1: Opening the last poem of Lamentations, the people who survived Jerusalem's fall speak together, asking God to take notice of their disgrace.
LAM.5.15: After listing the hardships of a conquered city, from young men at millstones to elders gone from the gate, the writer of Lamentations sums up what has been lost.
EZK.3.10: Having warned Ezekiel that Israel will be as stubborn with him as it has been with God, the Lord makes the new prophet's resolve harder than flint.
EZK.11.16: When people left in Jerusalem claim the exiles are far from God and have lost their share of the land, God answers through Ezekiel with a word for those exiles.
EZK.12.28: Hearing people shrug off Ezekiel's visions as being about the distant future, God tells the prophet how to answer them.
EZK.16.8: Continuing his long allegory, Ezekiel follows the baby God rescued from a field as she grows into a young woman, and describes the next time God passes by.
EZK.33.10: Right after reminding Ezekiel of his duty as Israel's watchman, God tells him to repeat back the hopeless words the people have been saying.
EZK.34.14: Picturing Israel's exiles as sheep led home from foreign countries, Ezekiel describes the land they will return to in terms any shepherd would love.
EZK.39.29: At the end of his vision of the defeat of Gog, a hostile invader from the north, Ezekiel records God's promise to gather every exile home.
DAN.4.27: After explaining King Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a great tree cut down, Daniel adds some personal advice to the king.
DAN.6.16: Unable to cancel his own decree despite struggling until sundown to save Daniel, King Darius gives way to the officials who trapped them both.
DAN.9.17: Recalling how God once rescued Israel from Egypt, Daniel pleads on behalf of a Jerusalem whose temple still lies in ruins.
1CO.2.3: Reminding the Corinthians of his first visit to their city, Paul admits he did not arrive as a confident, polished speaker.
DAN.10.17: Touched on the lips by a figure who looked like a man, Daniel finds his voice again but tells the heavenly visitor how drained he feels.
HOS.2.16: Playing on the word 'baal,' which meant both 'master' and the name of a Canaanite god, Hosea looks to a day when Israel will speak to God differently.
HOS.2.18: After promising to wipe the names of the Baals from Israel's lips, Hosea turns from the marriage picture to the land and every creature living in it.
HOS.11.11: Picturing God roaring like a lion to call his children home, Hosea describes how the scattered people of Israel will respond.
JOL.1.19: As locusts and drought leave cattle groaning and granaries empty, Joel turns from describing the devastation to crying out to God.
JOL.2.24: Turning to the farmers who had watched their crops vanish, Joel describes what harvest time will soon look like at the threshing floor and the press.
AMO.8.11: Warning Israel about a coming day of judgment when feasts will turn to mourning, Amos announces a deprivation stranger than any drought.
OBA.1.12: Obadiah rebukes Edom, descended from Jacob's brother Esau, for standing by while foreigners plundered Jerusalem.
OBA.1.15: After listing the ways Edom joined in Judah's ruin, from gloating to cutting off the fleeing survivors, Obadiah looks past Edom to the other nations.
JON.1.6: While a violent storm threatens to break apart the ship carrying Jonah away from God's call, the terrified captain finds the prophet asleep below deck.
JON.1.9: After the sailors' lots point to Jonah as the cause of the storm, they fire questions at him about who he is and where he comes from.
JON.1.16: Having thrown Jonah overboard and watched the raging sea grow suddenly calm, the pagan sailors respond in awe.
JON.3.5: Only one day into walking the vast city of Nineveh with his short warning of destruction, Jonah sees an unexpected response.
MIC.2.13: Right after promising to gather the remnant of Israel like a noisy flock in a pen, Micah describes that flock on the move.
MIC.6.4: In the courtroom scene Micah describes, God lays out his side of the case by pointing back to Israel's earliest history.
MIC.6.7: Pushing the worshiper's question further, Micah imagines offerings growing ever more extravagant and desperate.
MIC.7.14: Near the end of his book, Micah turns from promises of rebuilt walls to a prayer that God would care for his people like a shepherd.
NAM.1.12: In the middle of an oracle of doom against Nineveh, Assyria's capital, God turns briefly through Nahum to address the people of Judah.
GEN.21.1: After Sarah laughed at the idea of bearing a child in her old age, Genesis turns to the moment God's promise to her comes true.
ZEP.2.7: Among his warnings to the Philistine cities of the coast, Zephaniah includes a word about what will become of their land afterward.
ZEP.3.9: After announcing that God will gather the nations for judgment, Zephaniah surprisingly turns to what those same peoples will become.
HAG.1.4: In 520 BC, when the returned exiles in Jerusalem claimed it was not yet time to rebuild the temple, Haggai brings God's pointed response.
HAG.2.19: Speaking to the rebuilders of the temple on a specific day he wants them to remember, Haggai recalls the blight and meager harvests they had suffered.
ZEC.1.17: In the first of Zechariah's night visions, an angel tells the prophet to announce God's renewed compassion for a Jerusalem still recovering from its destruction.
ZEC.7.10: Continuing the Lord's summary of what the earlier prophets demanded, Zechariah names the vulnerable people the nation had been told never to exploit.
ZEC.8.4: Speaking to the few who had returned to a half-ruined Jerusalem, Zechariah passes on God's promise to come back and live in the city again.
ZEC.8.12: Recalling the lean, unsafe years before work on the temple resumed, God tells the returned remnant through Zechariah what the land will now give them.
ZEC.8.23: Closing a series of promises about Jerusalem's future, Zechariah foresees people from many nations eager to seek the God of Israel alongside his people.
ZEC.9.10: After God promises to camp around his house so that no oppressor overruns his people again, Zechariah looks further ahead to how far that peace will reach.
ZEC.10.1: Speaking to a farming people who depended on the spring rains, Zechariah tells them where to turn for the harvest they need.
ZEC.12.10: In a vision of a future day when God defends Jerusalem, Zechariah describes a sudden change of heart among the people toward someone they have wounded.
ZEC.14.9: Near the close of his book, after picturing living water flowing east and west from Jerusalem, Zechariah looks to the day God's rule is undisputed.
MAL.1.11: While rebuking priests who offered blind and lame animals on the altar, God declares through Malachi how differently the nations will one day honor his name.
ECC.9.1: Having searched in vain to understand all that God does under the sun, the Preacher reaches a conclusion about where the righteous and the wise stand.
MAL.4.4: After promising that those who fear him will trample the wicked like ashes, God speaks through Malachi about the foundation his people already have.
MAT.1.21: Appearing to Joseph in a dream as he considers quietly ending his engagement to Mary, an angel tells him about the child she is carrying.
MAT.5.11: Shifting from 'blessed are those' to 'blessed are you,' Jesus speaks directly to his own followers about the hostility they will face for his sake.
MAT.5.42: Having told his listeners to go a second mile for someone who forces them to go one, Jesus turns in the Sermon on the Mount to everyday requests from neighbors.
PRO.16.33: In ancient Israel, choices were often settled by casting lots, and Solomon ends a run of sayings with a word about who really decides the outcome.
MAT.8.13: In Capernaum, after a Roman centurion says Jesus need only give the word to heal his servant, Jesus answers the officer directly.
MAT.9.28: Two blind men have followed Jesus down the road calling him 'Son of David,' and when he goes indoors they come right in after him.
MAT.14.28: Of all the frightened disciples in the boat that night, it is Peter who answers Jesus, and he does it with a bold request.
MAT.15.25: Ignored at first and then told that Jesus was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, the foreign woman who has kept crying out after him near Tyre and Sidon drops to her knees.
MAT.18.4: With a child standing in the middle of the group, Jesus finishes answering his disciples' question about who ranks highest in the kingdom of heaven.
MAT.18.10: Having placed a child in front of his disciples, Jesus warns them against the attitude people often take toward the small and the overlooked.
MAT.18.19: After explaining how the church should deal with a member who sins and refuses to listen, Jesus goes on to speak about the authority he gives his disciples together.
MAT.18.15: Turning from parable to practice, Jesus tells his disciples the first step to take when a fellow believer wrongs them.
MAT.23.37: Ending a stinging series of woes against the scribes and Pharisees in the temple, Jesus suddenly voices his grief over the city of Jerusalem itself.
MAT.28.10: Running from the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary meet the risen Jesus on the way, and he sends word to the disciples who had deserted him.
MAT.28.18: Having sent word through the women that his brothers should meet him in Galilee, the risen Jesus now stands with the eleven on the mountain he had named.
MRK.1.4: Mark opens his Gospel not with Jesus' birth but with John the Baptist out in the wilderness near the Jordan, calling people to turn back to God.
MRK.1.38: When Simon and the others track Jesus down at his place of prayer and tell him everyone is looking for him, he points them somewhere else.
MRK.2.7: Some scribes sitting in the room bristle inwardly when Jesus tells a paralyzed man that his sins are forgiven.
MRK.2.15: Now a follower himself, Levi opens his home for a meal, and Jesus and his disciples share the table with people most religious teachers would avoid.
1JN.3.23: Explaining how believers can approach God with confidence, John sums up everything God asks of them in a single command with two parts.
MRK.4.37: At Jesus' suggestion, the disciples set out in the evening to cross the Sea of Galilee, taking him along in the boat he had been teaching from.
MRK.5.20: Left behind when Jesus sails away, the man once chained among the tombs faces the same neighbors who had just begged Jesus to leave their region.
MRK.6.29: After Herod has John the Baptist beheaded in prison to keep a rash promise made at his birthday banquet, John's followers hear the news.
MRK.8.17: Crossing the lake with one loaf aboard, the disciples miss Jesus' warning about the Pharisees and fret about bread, soon after he has fed two huge crowds.
MRK.8.29: On the way to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his disciples what people are saying about him, then makes the question personal.
MRK.9.7: On a high mountain where Jesus has been transfigured, Peter, too frightened to know what to say, has just offered to build shelters for Jesus, Moses and Elijah.
MRK.9.28: Earlier the disciples had tried and failed to free a boy from a spirit, so once they are alone indoors with Jesus they ask him about it.
1PE.4.16: Once he has warned that none of them should suffer as a thief or a meddler, Peter turns to the other kind of trouble his scattered readers are facing.
MRK.10.17: As Jesus heads out on the road again, a man who turns out to be very wealthy runs up and kneels in front of him.
MRK.10.28: After a rich man walks away from Jesus rather than part with his wealth, and Jesus remarks how hard that road is, Peter speaks up for the disciples.
MRK.10.31: Finishing his reply to Peter about what the disciples have given up to follow him, Jesus adds one more line about rank in God's kingdom.
MRK.10.52: Having flung aside his cloak and asked to see again, Bartimaeus hears Jesus' reply on the roadside outside Jericho.
ROM.6.8: Fresh from telling the Roman believers that their old self was crucified with Christ, Paul turns from the death they share with him to what comes after it.
MRK.12.42: Moments after warning about scribes who swallow up widows' houses, Jesus sits across from the temple treasury as many rich people make large gifts.
MRK.13.7: Sitting on the Mount of Olives across from the temple, Jesus answers Peter, James, John and Andrew when they ask privately about the signs of the end.
1CO.15.43: Answering Corinthians who doubted that the dead would rise, Paul compares a buried body to a seed that comes up transformed.
MRK.15.21: Mocked and beaten by the soldiers, Jesus is led out to be crucified, and a man coming in from the countryside is caught up in the moment.
MRK.15.38: At the very moment Jesus gives a loud cry and dies on the cross, something happens inside the temple in Jerusalem.
MRK.15.39: Standing directly in front of the cross, a Roman centurion sees how Jesus dies and reaches a verdict of his own.
MRK.15.43: As evening falls on the day Jesus dies, with the Sabbath about to begin, a respected member of the Jewish council takes a risk.
MRK.16.19: In the longer ending of Mark's Gospel, the risen Jesus finishes sending the eleven out to preach the good news to the whole world.
LUK.1.13: Chosen by lot to burn incense inside the temple, the elderly priest Zechariah is terrified when an angel appears beside the altar.
LUK.1.37: When Mary asks how she, a virgin, could bear a child, Gabriel points to her relative Elizabeth, pregnant in old age after years of being called barren.
LUK.1.50: Mary's song of praise, known as the Magnificat, widens here from her own story to God's dealings with his people across the ages.
LUK.1.64: When relatives want to name Elizabeth's baby after his father, Zechariah, mute since doubting the angel's message, writes out the name John.
LUK.3.11: When the crowds coming to be baptized by the Jordan ask John the Baptist how to show real repentance, he gives them a practical answer.
LUK.6.45: Continuing his Sermon on the Plain with images of trees and their fruit, Jesus draws the connection to what comes out of a person.
LUK.8.35: Word from the panicked pig herders brings the people of the Gerasene region out to see for themselves what Jesus has done.
LUK.10.6: Continuing his instructions to the followers he is sending ahead of him in pairs, Jesus prepares them for the different welcomes they will meet.
LUK.10.40: In a village home where she has welcomed Jesus as a guest, Martha is busy with the hosting while her sister sits listening at his feet.
LUK.11.1: Jesus has just finished praying somewhere along his journey toward Jerusalem when one of his disciples comes to him with a request.
LUK.15.2: As tax collectors and other known sinners crowd around to hear Jesus, the religious experts watching are scandalized by the company he keeps.
LUK.19.6: The crowd in Jericho has just heard Jesus invite himself to the home of a wealthy chief tax collector, and every eye turns to Zacchaeus.
LUK.19.38: Descending the Mount of Olives toward Jerusalem on a colt, Jesus is surrounded by a crowd of disciples praising God for all the miracles they have seen.
LUK.21.18: Having just told his disciples they may be betrayed by family and friends and even killed for his name, Jesus follows with a word of reassurance.
LUK.24.39: Startled disciples gathered in Jerusalem, joined by the two just back from Emmaus, cannot believe the risen Jesus is really standing in the room with them.
JHN.1.17: In the prologue to his Gospel, John sets the gift that came through Moses beside what has now arrived in Jesus.
JHN.1.48: Nathanael, who had doubted anything good could come from Nazareth, is startled when Jesus greets him as an honest Israelite before they have even met.
JHN.2.5: At a wedding in Cana where the wine has run out, Jesus' mother turns to the household servants even after Jesus seems to hold back.
JHN.4.29: After talking with Jesus at a well in Samaria, a woman leaves her water jar behind and hurries back into her town to tell the people.
JHN.4.50: In Cana, a royal official whose son lies dying in Capernaum pleads with Jesus to come quickly before it is too late.
JHN.6.11: On the grassy slopes by the Sea of Galilee, about five thousand men have been told to sit down, with only a boy's five loaves and two fish at hand.
JHN.6.63: In the synagogue at Capernaum, many of his followers find Jesus' talk of eating his flesh too hard to accept, and he answers their grumbling.
JHN.6.66: John records a turning point in Jesus' ministry, as his teaching on the bread of life divides the wider circle of people who had been following him.
JHN.8.31: During a tense debate in the temple courts, Jesus turns to the listeners who have begun to put their trust in him.
JHN.11.3: With their brother Lazarus seriously ill in Bethany, Mary and Martha send an urgent message to Jesus, who is some distance away.
JHN.14.8: Hearing Jesus say that knowing him means knowing the Father, Philip asks for something more concrete.
JHN.14.12: On his last night with them, Jesus tells his disciples that his going to the Father will not end the work he has been doing among them.
JHN.15.18: Right after telling his disciples to love one another, Jesus prepares them on his final night for the hostility they will meet.
JHN.16.27: Near the end of his farewell words on the night before his death, Jesus explains why his disciples will not need him to plead with the Father for them.
JHN.20.18: Sent by the risen Jesus with a message for his 'brothers,' Mary Magdalene leaves the garden tomb and goes to find the disciples.
ACT.1.7: Before Jesus leaves them, the apostles ask him whether this is the moment he will restore the kingdom to Israel.
