ACT.3.26: Speaking to the crowd at Solomon's Colonnade after a lame man is healed, Peter closes his sermon by reminding his fellow Israelites of God's promise to Abraham.
ACT.5.20: Jailed by the jealous high priest and his Sadducee allies, the apostles are led out during the night by an angel who gives them their next assignment.
ACT.6.8: Stephen, one of the seven men chosen to oversee the daily food distribution in the young Jerusalem church, soon stands out for more than serving tables.
ACT.8.22: In Samaria, after the former sorcerer Simon offers the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit, Peter answers him with blunt words.
ACT.9.13: Told in a vision to find Saul of Tarsus and restore his sight, the Damascus believer Ananias hesitates and reminds the Lord who this man is.
ACT.9.15: When Ananias protests that Saul has come to Damascus to arrest believers, the Lord answers with his plans for the very man Ananias fears.
ACT.9.22: Days after regaining his sight and being baptized, Saul begins preaching Jesus in the synagogues of Damascus, to the astonishment of those who knew his past.
ACT.9.40: In the upper room in Joppa where the body of the generous disciple Tabitha lies, the grieving widows have just shown Peter the clothes she made for them.
ACT.26.8: On trial before King Agrippa in Caesarea, Paul explains that he stands accused because of Israel's hope, and turns to the question at its center.
ACT.10.33: Cornelius, who had seen an angel while praying four days earlier, finishes telling Peter why he sent to Joppa for him, with relatives and friends gathered in Caesarea.
ACT.12.7: While the Jerusalem church keeps praying through the night, the story shifts from the praying believers to Peter's cell in Herod's prison.
ACT.13.43: In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, Paul has just preached that forgiveness comes through Jesus, and many listeners are eager to hear more.
ACT.15.8: Standing up after long debate among the apostles and elders, Peter recalls how God first brought Gentiles to faith through his preaching.
ACT.16.5: Now joined by young Timothy from Lystra, Paul and Silas travel from town to town sharing the Jerusalem council's decisions with the churches.
1CH.22.18: Near the end of his life, David charges Israel's leaders to help his son Solomon build the temple that David himself was not allowed to build.
ACT.17.24: Starting from an Athenian altar inscribed to an unknown god, Paul begins telling the city's thinkers who that God really is.
EXO.34.21: On Mount Sinai, as God renews his covenant with Israel after the golden calf, he restates the Sabbath rest for a people who would soon farm their own land.
DAN.6.3: Serving as one of three chief administrators under King Darius, the exiled Daniel begins to stand out from all the other royal officials.
ROM.2.4: Turning to readers who condemn others for sins they commit themselves, Paul challenges how they are treating God's patience toward them.
ROM.6.17: Picturing sin and righteousness as two masters competing for a person's service, Paul pauses to thank God for how the Roman believers answered the gospel.
ROM.8.33: Using the language of a courtroom, Paul imagines someone trying to press charges against the people God has chosen for himself.
1CO.1.10: Having heard of quarrels in Corinth from members of Chloe's household, Paul makes the first appeal of his letter, calling the church to unity.
1CO.4.7: Confronting Corinthian believers who took pride in siding with one teacher over another, Paul punctures their sense of superiority with a string of questions.
1CO.6.7: Troubled that believers in Corinth were taking one another to court before unbelieving judges, Paul questions why they are so determined to win.
1CO.6.11: After listing the kinds of wrongdoers who will not inherit God's kingdom, Paul reminds the Corinthians that some of them once lived exactly that way.
1CO.8.1: Turning to a dispute in Corinth over eating meat that had been sacrificed to idols, Paul begins with a word to those proud of what they know.
2CO.1.5: Right after blessing the God who comforts him so that he can comfort others, Paul tells the Corinthians what his own troubles have in common with Christ's.
2CO.2.4: Explaining why he chose to write rather than make another painful visit to Corinth, Paul tells the church what that letter cost him.
2CO.2.13: Recalling an open door for preaching in the port city of Troas, Paul explains why he moved on while waiting for Titus to bring news from Corinth.
2CO.3.5: Answering critics who expected letters of recommendation, Paul calls the Corinthian believers his real credentials, then says where his confidence actually comes from.
2CO.4.15: Having described being hard pressed, persecuted and struck down for Jesus' sake, Paul tells the Corinthians whose benefit all of it serves.
2CO.5.15: Reasoning from his conviction that Christ died for all, Paul spells out for the Corinthians what that death means for everyone who is still living.
2CO.7.5: Picking his travel story back up after a long digression, Paul describes the state he and his companions were in when they reached Macedonia.
2CO.8.16: Sending Titus back to Corinth to help finish gathering a gift for needy believers, Paul vouches for his coworker's genuine care for the church.
2CO.9.10: Quoting a psalm about the generous person who scatters gifts to the poor, Paul carries its farming picture further for the Corinthians collecting for Jerusalem.
2CO.13.4: Preparing for a third visit to Corinth, where some demanded proof that Christ really spoke through him, Paul answers the charge that he is weak.
GAL.1.23: Recounting his first years after meeting Christ, Paul notes that the churches of Judea knew him only by reputation, and repeats what they were saying.
GAL.3.14: Tracing God's ancient promise to Abraham forward to his non-Jewish readers in Galatia, Paul names what Christ's death on the cross opened up for them.
GAL.4.16: Hurt that the Galatians, who once would have given him their own eyes, had turned cold toward him, Paul confronts the change head-on.
GAL.4.28: Drawing an allegory from Abraham's two sons and their mothers, Hagar and Sarah, Paul tells the Galatians which son they resemble.
GAL.5.15: Having summed up the whole law in the command to love your neighbor, Paul turns to the infighting he feared among the Galatian churches.
GAL.5.24: Having set the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, Paul tells the Galatians where people who belong to Christ now stand.
GAL.6.17: Ending a letter full of controversy over circumcision, Paul makes one last personal request of the Galatians before his closing blessing.
EPH.1.7: In the middle of one long sentence of praise, Paul moves from God's plan to adopt believers as his children to what Christ's death accomplished for them.
EPH.2.17: Describing what Christ did for both Jews and Gentiles, Paul borrows language from Isaiah about people who are far away and people who are near.
EPH.2.18: For non-Jewish readers who had once been strangers to Israel's God, Paul describes what Christ has opened up for them and for Jewish believers alike.
EPH.3.7: Explaining the once-hidden mystery that Gentiles share fully in God's promises, Paul describes how he himself came to carry that message.
EPH.4.16: Finishing a long thought about the gifts Christ gives to his church, Paul compares the whole community of believers to a living body.
EPH.5.18: Among practical instructions for believers living in a pagan city, Paul contrasts two very different things a person can be filled with.
EPH.6.16: Working through a soldier's equipment piece by piece, Paul has named the belt, the breastplate and the footwear before turning to the shield.
EPH.6.17: For the final pieces of God's armor, Paul names protection for the head and a weapon for the hand, and says what each one is.
PHP.1.7: Having just voiced confidence in God's work among the Philippians, Paul explains why he feels so deeply attached to them.
PHP.1.12: Turning from his prayer for the Philippians to news of his own situation, Paul begins to update them on his imprisonment.
PHP.2.17: Aware that his imprisonment might end in his death, Paul tells the Philippians how he feels about that prospect.
PHP.3.18: After asking the Philippians to imitate him and others who live the same way, Paul grows emotional as he warns them about a very different example.
PHP.4.2: Two women in the Philippian church who had once labored beside Paul for the gospel had fallen into disagreement, and he appeals to them personally.
PHP.4.14: Careful not to sound ungrateful after saying he can manage in any situation, Paul affirms the Philippians for the gift they sent him in prison.
ROM.5.11: Rounding off a run of 'how much more' arguments about Christ's death, Paul adds a note of present-day joy for the believers in Rome.
COL.1.15: Having thanked the Father for bringing believers into the kingdom of his beloved Son, Paul begins a sweeping description of who that Son is.
COL.1.28: Commissioned by God as a servant of the church, Paul sums up how he and his fellow workers make Christ known and what they are aiming for.
COL.2.16: Facing teachers in Colossae who insisted on special diets and religious calendars, Paul draws a practical conclusion from Christ's victory on the cross.
1TH.2.2: Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed in Philippi shortly before reaching Thessalonica, and Paul reminds the church how that first visit began.
1TH.2.19: Looking ahead to the Lord's return, Paul asks the young church in Thessalonica a question about what will make all his work worthwhile.
1TH.3.10: Though cheered by Timothy's report, Paul still wants to finish what he started in Thessalonica, and he tells the believers how he prays about it.
1TH.3.11: Still unable to travel back to Thessalonica, Paul turns from describing his prayers to praying one aloud in the letter itself.
1TH.4.16: Having promised that the living will not go ahead of believers who have died, Paul describes the sounds that will announce the Lord's arrival.
2TH.3.10: Some believers in Thessalonica had stopped working and were living off others, so Paul reminds the church of a rule he had given them in person.
2TH.3.15: After telling the church to keep away from any idle believer who ignores this letter's instructions, Paul adds how they should still treat such a person.
1TI.4.10: Explaining to Timothy why he and his coworkers keep pushing through toil and criticism, Paul names the one they have staked everything on.
1TI.4.13: Timothy had been left in Ephesus while Paul traveled on, and here he is told what to prioritize in the church until Paul returns.
1TI.4.16: Wrapping up a series of personal charges to his young coworker, Paul tells Timothy what is at stake in how he lives and teaches.
1TI.5.25: In advice to Timothy about church elders, including not laying hands on anyone too hastily, Paul notes that some people's sins are not obvious at first.
2TI.1.3: Right after his greeting, Paul begins this deeply personal letter to Timothy the way he began many others, with thanks to God.
2TI.1.13: Shifting from his own confidence to Timothy's responsibility, Paul reminds his younger coworker of the teaching he heard directly from him.
2TI.1.16: Stung that so many in the province of Asia had abandoned him, Paul singles out one friend's household that did the opposite.
2TI.2.7: After packing a soldier, an athlete and a farmer into three quick comparisons, Paul asks Timothy to think them through.
2TI.2.10: Chained like a criminal yet insisting that God's word cannot be chained, Paul tells Timothy who his suffering is for.
PHM.1.18: In his letter to Philemon, Paul is sending Onesimus back to the master he had been separated from, and he takes up the matter of anything Onesimus owes.
HEB.1.3: Contrasting God's past messages through the prophets with his final word through his Son, the writer of Hebrews opens the letter by describing who that Son is.
HEB.1.14: After quoting a string of Old Testament passages to show the Son is greater than the angels, the writer of Hebrews turns to what the angels are for.
HEB.2.17: Explaining why the Son shared fully in human flesh and blood, the writer of Hebrews introduces Jesus as high priest, a theme the rest of the letter develops.
HEB.5.7: Having shown that Christ did not appoint himself high priest, the writer of Hebrews recalls the kind of anguished praying the Gospels describe in Gethsemane.
HEB.5.8: Still dwelling on Jesus' life on earth, the writer of Hebrews makes a striking claim about what God's own Son went through.
HEB.11.11: Moving from Abraham's journeys to his household, the writer of Hebrews turns to his wife, who had waited many years for the son God promised.
HEB.12.7: Having quoted Proverbs about the Lord correcting those he loves, the writer of Hebrews applies it to readers growing weary under opposition.
HEB.13.7: In a run of short closing instructions, the writer of Hebrews turns readers' thoughts to the people who first taught them God's word.
JAS.1.9: Turning from prayer for wisdom to the gap between rich and poor in the church, James first speaks to believers of humble means.
JAS.1.13: Having praised those who endure testing, James heads off an excuse people are quick to make when they give in to temptation.
JAS.1.18: Contrasting desire that gives birth to sin and death with the unchanging Father of lights, James tells his readers what that Father chose to do for them.
JAS.1.25: Having pictured someone who glances in a mirror and immediately forgets his own face, James describes the opposite kind of person.
JAS.2.5: Rebuking a congregation that gave the best seats to the rich and made the poor stand, James asks them a pointed question about whom God has chosen.
JAS.3.2: Right after cautioning that few should become teachers because they will be judged more strictly, James includes himself among those who fail.
JAS.3.13: After lamenting that blessing and cursing pour from the same mouth, James shifts from speech to the kind of life that proves real wisdom.
JAS.3.16: Warning that bitter rivalry in the heart is nothing to boast about, James looks at what happens to a community where it is allowed to grow.
JAS.4.1: Moving from his praise of peacemakers to the fights breaking out among his readers, James asks a blunt question about where they come from.
JAS.4.6: Right after rebuking readers for their worldly cravings and divided loyalty, James turns to God's grace and quotes a line from Proverbs.
JAS.5.14: After telling the suffering to pray and the cheerful to sing, James takes up a third case: a believer laid low by illness.
1PE.1.17: Right after quoting God's call to be holy because he is holy, Peter reminds his scattered readers who it is they pray to.
1PE.1.21: Having described Christ as a spotless lamb known before the world began, Peter traces where his readers' trust ultimately rests.
1PE.2.11: Turning from who believers are to how they should live among neighbors who slander them, Peter opens a new section with a personal appeal.
1PE.5.4: Speaking as a fellow elder to the church leaders who shepherd God's flock, Peter looks ahead to the reward awaiting them.
1PE.5.12: Adding a personal note at the very end, Peter mentions the coworker who helped with the letter and sums up why he wrote it.
2PE.1.4: Before he lists the qualities his readers should add to their faith, Peter explains what God has already set in motion for them.
2PE.1.21: Anticipating the false teachers he is about to warn against, Peter tells his readers where the prophets' words in Scripture really came from.
1JN.1.8: In a series of 'if we say' statements weighing people's claims against their lives, John turns to a claim some were making about sin.
1JN.2.2: Still reassuring believers who have sinned, John widens the scope of what Jesus Christ, the Righteous One, has done.
1JN.2.6: Offering practical tests for anyone who claims to know God, John moves from keeping his commandments to the example Jesus left.
1JN.2.10: Contrasting a darkness that is passing away with the true light already shining, John takes up how believers treat one another.
1JN.2.28: After warning about people trying to lead his readers astray, John turns their eyes toward the day Christ appears.
1JN.3.14: After recalling Cain's murder of his brother and warning that the world may hate them, John gives his readers a way to know where they stand.
1JN.3.17: Moving from the ultimate sacrifice to a far more ordinary test, John pictures a comfortable believer face to face with someone in need.
1JN.4.14: Speaking for those who had seen Jesus with their own eyes, John adds personal testimony to his reflections on God's love.
1JN.4.17: Bringing his reflection on living in God's love to a point, John turns to how believers can face the day of judgment.
1JN.5.5: With false teachers denying the truth about Jesus in view, John poses a question about who truly wins against the world.
1JN.5.18: Having urged his readers to pray for a fellow believer caught in sin, John closes his letter with a set of things he wants them to be sure of.
REV.3.21: In the last of the seven messages to the churches of Asia, the risen Jesus closes with his final promise to the church in Laodicea.
REV.15.4: In John's vision, those who conquered the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, singing the song of Moses and the Lamb.
